entities, seeking verification, computation and release of
their outstanding salary dues along with consequential
benefits. 
Heard the learned Amicus Curiae as well as the learned
Senior counsel and the learned counsel appearing for the
parties. 
It is submitted that it would be impossible for the
learned  Amicus  Curiae  to  undertake  the  exercise  of
verifying  and  computing  the  aforesaid  claims  of  the
applicants due to the voluminous nature of the records
involved, and that a Committee may be appointed to conduct
the said exercise.
In such view of the matter, we deem it appropriate
to constitute a Committee to undertake the exercise of
verification  and  computation  of  the  claims  of  the
aforesaid  applicants.  Accordingly,  it  is  directed  as
follows: 
50

## Page 96

CONMT.PET.(C) No. 1820-1822/2017
1. The Committee shall be chaired by Hon’ble Mr Justice
Rajiv Sahai Endlaw, retired Judge of the High Court. The
Chairperson  shall  be  entitled  to  an  honorarium  of
5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs only) per month.₹
2. The Chairperson shall be at liberty to seek the
assistance of such persons as he may deem necessary for
the effective discharge of the Committee's functions. Such
assistance  may  include  officers  from  the  District
Judiciary,  Chartered  Accountants,  or  any  other  person
possessing  the  requisite  expertise.  Every  person  so
engaged  by  the  Chairperson  shall  be  entitled  to  an
honorarium of 2,50,000/- (Rupees Two Lakhs Fifty Thousand₹
only) per month. 
3. The Committee shall be at liberty to engage any
additional personnel or support staff as may be necessary
for the expeditious completion of the exercise.
4.  In  addition  to  the  remuneration  expenses  of  the
members of the Committee, an amount of Rs. 25,00,000/-
(Rupees Twenty-Five Lakhs only) shall be made available
towards  all  incidental  and  administrative  expenses
connected with the functioning of the Committee. 
5.  The  learned  Chairperson  of  the  Committee  shall
coordinate with the learned Amicus Curiae to facilitate
the release of funds from the ‘SEBI-Sahara Refund Account’
held  by  the  SEBI,  towards  the  remuneration  and
administrative expenses of the Committee. 
51

## Page 97

CONMT.PET.(C) No. 1820-1822/2017
6. The Committee shall be at liberty to devise and adopt
its  own  procedure  for  conducting  the  exercise  of
verification and quantification of claims, in accordance
with law. 
7.  We  make  it  clear  that  the  Committee  shall  only
consider the claims of those persons whose applications
have been taken on record vide this order. The Registry is
directed to furnish to the Chairperson a copy of the list
filed  by  the  learned  Amicus  Curiae  containing  the
particulars of all such applications.  
8. The Sahara Group and all concerned stakeholders shall
extend their full support and cooperation to the Committee
and shall furnish all records, documents, accounts and
such other material as may be required by the Committee
for verification and quantification of the claims.
9.  The  Committee  shall  complete  the  exercise  of
verification  of  the  claims  and  quantification  of  the
amounts payable, within a period of three months from the
date of commencement of its functioning and shall submit
its report to this Court. Upon receipt of the aforesaid
report, appropriate orders regarding the release of the
amounts shall be passed by this Court.
List  after  the  receipt  of  the  report  of  the
Committee.
(KRITIKA TIWARI)                                 (POONAM VAID)

I.A. No. 207972 of 2026 – Application seeking 
recall/expunction  
 
1. The instant application has been filed by 
respondent No. 4 – Bombay Burmah Trading 
Corporation Limited (BBTCL), seeking 
recall/expunction of the observations and directions 
contained in paragraph 59 of the order dated 29 th 
May, 2026 passed by this Court. 

## Page 127

2 
 
2. Paragraph 59 of the aforesaid order reads as 
follows: 
“59. Further, the massive lease rent liability 
computed against BBTC Ltd. amounting to Rs. 
4,655,24,33,533.21 (Rupees Four Thousand Six 
Hundred Fifty -Five Crore Twenty -Four Lakh 
Thirty-Three Thousand Five Hundred Thirty -
Three and Paise Twenty-One only) remains to be 
recovered, and the State must take expeditious 
steps in this regard in accordance with the 
orders of the Madras High Court. We expect to 
receive a compliance report in this regard by next 
date. Further, we shall consider the partial 
utilization of t his amount towards the 
Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management 
and Planning Authority (CAMPA) fund.” 
 
3. Mr. Darius Khambata, learned senior counsel 
appearing for respondent No. 4 – BBTCL, submitted 
that the aforesaid observations were based on the 
Second Report (Report No. 02 of 2026) dated 16 th 
January, 2026 submitted by the CEC, wherein it was 
noted that an amount of Rs. 4,655.24 crores had 
been finally determined as lease rent payable by 
BBTCL and that the said amount was due and 
recoverable from BBTCL. It was submitted that no 
such demand or computation had ever been served 
upon BBTCL, nor had BBTCL been afforded any 
opportunity to contest the said computation. 

## Page 128

3 
 
4. Learned senior counsel further submitted that 
the aforesaid amount finds mention only in an 
internal communication dated 10 th October, 2025  
addressed by the Deputy Director/Wildlife Warden to 
the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests and Head 
of Forest Force, Tamil Nadu. The said communication 
merely forwarded a draft lease -rent notice and 
calculation sheet for obtaining Government approval 
before any formal demand could be raised against 
BBTCL. It was therefore urged that the amount could 
not be treated as a crystallised or recoverable 
liability.  
5. Learned senior counsel contended that the 
Madras High Court, vide order dated 18 th August, 
2025 passed in W.A. No. 1435 of 2017 and connected 
matters, had set aside the earlier lease-rent demands 
and granted liberty to the authorities to re -quantify 
the lease rent, subject to issuance of a fresh notice to 
BBTCL and affording it a full opportunity of hearing, 
including an opportunity to contest the demand on 
merits and on the question of jurisdiction.  
6. Learned senior counsel further contended that, 
pursuant to the said order, no fresh notice was served 
upon BBTCL, no hearing was afforded to it and no 

## Page 129

4 
 
final order determining the re -quantified lease rent 
was passed. Consequently, on the date of order dated 
29th May, 2026, there was no subsisting demand 
capable of recovery.  
7. Shri K. Parmeshwar, learned Amicus Curiae , 
supported the submissions advanced on behalf of 
BBTCL. He also agreed that the lease-rent amount of 
Rs. 4,655.24 crore had not been communicated to 
BBTCL by way of any notice and that the said figure 
appeared only in the internal communication of the 
authorities. It was further submitted that the order 
dated 18th August, 2025 passed by the Madras High 
Court contemplates a fresh determination only after 
due notice and hearing to BBTCL. 
8. Having considered the submissions advanced 
by learned senior counsel appearing for BBTCL and 
learned Amicus Curiae and having regard to the fact 
that the amount of Rs. 4,655.24 crore had neither 
been the subject matter of a notice served upon 
BBTCL nor been finally determined after affording 
BBTCL an opportunity of hearing, we are of the view 
that the observations con tained in paragraph 59 of 
the order dated 29th May, 2026 warrant recall. 

## Page 130

5 
 
9. Accordingly, observations made in paragraph 
59 of the order dated 29 th May, 2026 to the extent, 
the same refer to the lease rent liability of BBTCL, are 
recalled. 
10. However, we make it clear that the State 
Government shall recompute/re -quantify the lease 
rent, in accordance with the order dated 18th August, 
2025 passed by the Madras High Court in W.A. No. 
1435 of 2017 and connected matters, after issuing 
due notice to BBTCL and affording it an opportunity 
of hearing in accordance with law.  
11. In view of the aforesaid observations, the I.A. 
stands disposed of. 
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). 6395-6397 OF 2025 
12. This Court vide order dated 29 th May, 2026 
passed the following directions: - 
“66. In view of the foregoing discussion, this Court 
is of the opinion that, despite the steps taken by 
the State, the matter requires a structured, time 
bound and closely monitored framework to ensure 
effective implementation and consequences for 
noncompliance. The assurances and commitments 
made in the reply  affidavit must translate into 
concrete, measurable and verifiable action on the 
ground through effective monitoring, institutional 
accountability and sustained enforcement. 
Accordingly, we issue the following directions:  
 

## Page 131

6 
 
i. A time -bound, division -wise 
encroachment eviction plan shall be 
prepared and implemented on priority, with 
clearly defined timelines, measurable 
milestones, and designated officerlevel 
responsibilities. The said plan shall be 
placed before CEC within a per iod of one 
month.  
ii. The eviction plan shall include 
comprehensive measures for physical 
eviction, rehabilitation wherever applicable, 
legal action against wilful violators, and 
post-eviction ecological restoration, so as to 
ensure that reclaimed forest land is not re -
encroached. Any failure to comply with the 
approved plan shall invite administrative 
accountability at the highest level.  
iii. The State Law Department shall 
continuously monitor all proceedings 
relating to encroachments pending before 
district courts and other judicial forums 
and take appropriate measures for their 
expeditious disposal. The status of all 
pending cases relating to  the 
encroachments before various forums shall 
be submitted for perusal of this Court in a 
tabular form supported by an affidavit on 
the next date of hearing.  
iv. Disciplinary and legal action shall be 
initiated against all identified 118 
Government servants found to be 
encroachers, in accordance with Rule 3 of 
the Tamil Nadu Government Servants’ 
Conduct Rules, 1973 and other applicable 
laws. We further direct that the State 
Government shall consider imposing 
additional penalties on all present and 
former Government employees found to be 
encroachers, and require such persons to 
deposit appropriate environmental 
restitution and restoration charges with the 

## Page 132

7 
 
Tamil Nadu State Compensatory 
Afforestation Fund Management and 
Planning Authority (CAMPA). The amounts 
so deposited shall be maintained separately 
and utilised exclusively for ecological 
restoration, habitat recovery, afforestation, 
forest protection and related conservation 
measures in the affected areas, in 
accordance with the Compensatory 
Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 and the Rules 
framed thereunder.  
v. A blanket moratorium shall be 
imposed on the extension of welfare 
schemes, public utilities, transport 
facilities, electricity supply, and 
infrastructure support within encroached 
forest areas, so as to ensure that illegal 
occupation is neither incentivise d nor 
legitimised.  
vi. There shall be a complete prohibition 
on approval or commencement of any new 
non-forestry activity or diversion proposal 
within the entire Agasthyamalai  landscape 
under the provisions of the Forest 
(Conservation) Act, 1980, until all 
encroachments are removed and all illegal 
infrastructure is dismantled or otherwise 
dealt with strictly in accordance with extant 
law, rules and regulations. Proposal for 
regularization, if any, shall be placed before 
the CEC which shall examine the same and 
submit its opinion to this Court for further 
directions.  
vii. Stringent disciplinary, penal, and 
criminal action shall be proposed against all 
officials, officers, and Heads of Departments 
who commenced, facilitated, approved, or 
permitted illegal infrastructure works 
within the forest areas, specially within the 
Megamalai Wildlife Sanctuary, and 
generally within the Agasthyamalai 

## Page 133

8 
 
Biosphere in violation of the Forest 
(Conservation) Act, 1980. A comprehensive 
status report regarding such action shall be 
filed with the CEC within three months.  
viii. All Government establishments, 
facilities, and unauthorised infrastructure 
situated within forest areas, including 
within the Srivilliputhur – Megamalai Tiger 
Reserve, shall be discontinued, relocated, 
dismantled, and removed from forest land 
within a period of six months.  
ix. All illegal resorts, commercial 
establishments, and tourism -related 
infrastructure operating within the 
Megamalai area and other forest lands shall 
be made non -operational forthwith and 
dismantled in accordance with law and by 
ensuring minimum disruption to the forest 
area. All electricity connections and 
unauthorised transmission lines servicing 
such encroachments s hall also be 
disconnected and removed forthwith. The 
aforesaid procedure shall be carried out in 
the supervision of the CEC. 
x. The Chief Secretary, Government of

survey records, settlement records, and 
land documents pertaining to the 
Kanyakumari Wildlife Sanctuary presently 
in Kerala’s custody are transferred to the 
Tamil Nadu Forest Department within three 
months. The Chief Secretary, Government 
of Tamil Nadu, shall coordinate with the 
Government of Kerala to ensure expeditious 
compliance.  
xi. The Forest Survey of India (FSI) under 
the Ministry of Environment, Forest and

digitisation of the entire boundary of the 
Kalakkad Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve,

removal of encroachments pursuant to the 
aforesaid directions shall be protected from 
prosecution in relation to bona fide actions 
taken by them during the aforesaid 
exercise, except in cases involving mala fide, 
arbitrary action or abuse of authority. xiv. 
In case the State Government fails to ensure 
compliance with the above directions, the 
CEC may recommend deployment of 
paramilitary forces for providing assistance 
to carry out the exercise of removal of 
encroachments.  
xiii. The States shall submit monthly 
compliance reports to the CEC. The CEC 
shall undertake ground verification and 
submit quarterly status reports before this 
Court until all directions are fully complied 
with to the satisfaction of this Court.” 
 

## Page 135

10 
 
13. Pursuant to aforesaid order, the CEC has 
submitted its Report (Report No. 21 of 2026)1 and an 
affidavit has been filed by the State of Tamil Nadu. 
14. We have heard Shri K. Parmeshwar, learned 
Amicus Curiae, Shri Jaideep Gupta, learned senior 
counsel appearing for the State of Tamil Nadu, and 
Mr. Shriram Panchu, learned senior counsel 
appearing for the impleader - Department of Social 
Justice, State of Tamil Nadu. We have also perused 
the affidavit filed by the State of Tamil Nadu and have 
gone through the CEC Report.  
15. The affidavit filed by the State of Tamil Nadu 
sets out the steps taken pursuant to the directions of 
this Court. Multi -departmental teams comprising 
officials of the Survey, Forest and Police Departments 
have been constituted for survey and identification of 
encroachments, and a drone -based survey covering 
approximately 900 hectares has been undertaken. 
The State has also taken action against 15 illegal 
resorts in Megamalai , including disconnection of 
electricity and stoppage of their operations, though 
some were subsequently de -sealed pursuant to 
 
1 Hereinafter, referred to as “CEC Report”. 

## Page 136

11 
 
orders passed by the Madras High Court. Notices 
have been issued to encroachers in different forest 
ranges, and 52 encroachers in the Megamalai Range 
have been evicted. The State has identified 118 
Government servants as occupying forest land and 
has furnished particulars regarding the notices 
issued to them and those which remain pending, 
have been returned or refused. The State has also 
referred to the protests by local inhabitants seeking 
grant of pattas and protection of their livelihood.  
16. The State has relied upon historical maps, 
revenue records, Zamin grazing permits and census 
records to show that habitation and cultivation in 
portions of the area pre -dated their subsequent 
declaration as Reserved Forest and Wildlife 
Sanctuary. In partic ular, reliance has been placed 
upon the 1912 and 1931 maps, grazing permits of 
1937 and 1951 and the 1961 Census records relating 
to Narasingapuram , as also the subsequent 
notifications and re -classification of the lands. The 
State has submitted that these records demonstrate 
that certain persons have genuine and long-standing 
rights in the area and that their occupation cannot, 
in all cases, be treated as wilful encroachment. In this 

## Page 137

12 
 
regard, the State has also referred to the Scheduled 
Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers 
(Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 2, under 
which 122 individual forest rights have already been 
recognised and pattas granted across four villages, 
while 398 individual claims remain pending or under 
verification across 16 villages. Community rights 
have also been recognised in nine panchayat villages.  
17. The State has sought to distinguish between 
persons whose forest rights have been recognised or 
are being considered under the statutory framework, 
long-standing inhabitants dependent upon the forest 
land for their livelihood, and persons who are 
unauthorised encroachers. With regard to  the cash-
crop cultivation, the State has submitted that crops 
such as silk cotton and cashew were promoted under 
Government schemes in the past and that local 
inhabitants have traditionally depended upon such 
cultivation for their livelihood. The State ha s also 
referred to the historical grant of pattas in respect of 
certain lands and submitted that these aspects 
 
2 For short, “Forest Rights Act, 2006”. 

## Page 138

13 
 
require consideration before all occupants are 
uniformly treated as wilful illegal encroachers. 
18. The CEC Report, however, indicates that 
substantial compliance with the directions issued by 
this Court is yet to be achieved. The CEC has noted 
that despite the identification of a large number of  
encroachments, actual physical eviction and recovery 
of forest land remain limited. It has also noted 
continuing encroachments, unauthorised structures 
and cultivation within forest areas and has raised 
specific concerns regarding the action taken against  
Government servants identified as encroachers. The 
CEC has accordingly assessed several aspects of 
compliance as “Not Complete” or “Partially 
Complete.” 
19. Shri Jaideep Gupta, learned senior counsel 
appearing for the State of Tamil Nadu, submitted that 
the State has taken substantial steps towards 
compliance with the directions issued by this Court 
and is proceeding with the survey, identification and 
removal of encroachments in a phased manner. He 
submitted that the exercise involves a large area and 
a considerable number of inhabitants and, therefore, 
requires proper identification of the nature and 

## Page 139

14 
 
status of the occupation before eviction is 
undertaken. He submitted that, out of the 118 
Government servants identified as encroachers, 
notices could so far be served upon only 20, and the 
State is taking steps for service upon the remaining 
persons.  
20. Learned senior counsel drew attention to the 
historical revenue records, maps, Zamin records and 
census material relied upon in the affidavit to submit 
that habitation and cultivation in portions of the area 
existed prior to their declaration as Reserved F orest. 
He submitted that the State has also taken action  
against illegal resorts and encroachers and that 
electricity supply to the illegal resorts has since been 
disconnected. He further submitted that the District 
Collector has not given any assurance that pattas 
would be granted to the inhabitants. It was urged 
that a harmonious approach is required, whereby the 
ecological protection of the forest is ensured while, at 
the same time, due consideration is given to the 
claims of bona fide inhabitants who have been 
residing in the area for a considerable period. He 
accordingly sought reasonable time to complete the 
exercise in accordance with law. 

## Page 140

15 
 
21. Mr. Shriram Panchu, learned senior counsel 
appearing for the impleader, Department of Social 
Justice, State of Tamil Nadu submitted that all 
persons presently residing in the area cannot be 
treated uniformly as illegal encroachers, particularly 
when the material on record demonstrates long -
standing habitation and cultivation and the 
dependence of a section of the inhabitants upon the 
land for their livelihood. Placing reliance upon the 
historical records and the rights already recognised, 
including the pattas granted under the Forest Rights 
Act, 2006, he submitted that the statutory rights of 
eligible inhabitants require due consideration. He 
further submitted that the Forest Rights Act, 2006 
itself prescribes a procedure for determination and 
recognition of f orest rights of persons satisfying the 
statutory requirements, and that such claims are 
required to be examined by the competent authorities 
in accordance with the procedure prescribed under 
the Act before coercive action is taken against 
persons claiming such rights. 
22. Per contra, Shri K. Parmeshwar, learned Amicus 
Curiae, submitted that the directions issued by this 
Court vide order dated 29th May, 2026 were required 

## Page 141

16 
 
to be implemented in their letter and spirit and that 
the material placed before the Court demonstrates 
that actual eviction and recovery of forest land 
remain substantially incomplete. He submitted that 
preparation of plans, issuance of notices and 
identification of encroachments shows lethargic 
approach and cannot by themselves constitute 
compliance with the directions of this Court. 
23. Learned Amicus further submitted that silk 
cotton cultivation is being rampantly promoted 
within the Reserved Forest area, and that such 
cultivation is not merely attributable to local 
inhabitants but is being undertaken at the instance 
of outside forces/persons. He submitted that the 
nature and extent of such cultivation and the persons 
behind it require thorough investigation, particularly 
in view of the ecological consequences of cultivation 
within the Reserved Forest. It was urged that the 
issue of pattas allegedly granted by the District 
Collector in respect of lands falling within the area in 
question requires examination, particularly as to the 
authority under which such pattas were granted and 
the status of the lands at the time of such grant. 

## Page 142

17 
 
24. We have considered the submissions advanced 
by learned senior counsel and perused the material 
placed before us.  
25. At this stage, we do not propose to express any 
opinion on the merits of the competing claims or on 
the correctness of the respective positions reflected in 
the affidavit of the State and the report of the CEC. 
However, certain issues emerging from the mat erial 
before us require a specific and detailed response 
from the State.  
26. In particular, the issue relating to silk cotton 
cultivation within the Reserved Forest area, the 
circumstances in which such cultivation is being 
carried on and the role, if any, of persons from 
outside the area; the grant of pattas by the District 
Collector in respect of lands falling within the area in 
question; and the action taken against the 118 
Government servants identified as encroachers, 
require serious emergent consideration.  
27. We are also of the view that, before proceeding 
further, it is necessary for the State to respond 
specifically to the observations contained in CEC 
Report, particularly those observations which have 

## Page 143

18 
 
been categorised by the CEC as “Not Complete” or 
“Partially Complete”.  
28. There is another aspect which, in our view, 
requires independent consideration. In view of the  
act that M/s Bombay Burma  Trading Corporation 
Limited (BBTCL) had been carrying on extensive  tea 
plantation activities deep within the forest landscape 
and having  regard to the ecologically sensitive 
character of the area, we consider it  necessary that 
the environmental consequences of such plantation  
activities be independently assessed in a 
comprehensive and scientific manner. 
29. Accordingly, the CEC shall examine, inter alia, 
the manner and  extent of use of insecticides, 
pesticides, fungicides, herbicides and other  agro-
chemicals by the Tea Company during the period of 
its operation,  the nature and quantity of such 
chemicals used, the manner of their application and 
disposal, and their potential impact upon the soil, 
surface and ground water, natural vegetation, flora, 
fauna and the overall ecological integrity of the forest 
ecosystem. The CEC shall, for this  purpose, obtain 
and examine the relevant records of the Tea Company 

## Page 144

19 
 
and the concerned authorities and, wherever 
considered necessary,  undertake or cause to be 
undertaken appropriate scientific sampling,  
laboratory analysis, field studies and ecological 
assessment so as to  ascertain whether any 
contamination, degradation or adverse ecological  
impact has occurred and, if so, the nature, extent and 
duration thereof. The CEC shall further assess the 
extent of ecological restoration  required, the cost 
thereof, and the environmental compensation or  
compensatory amount, if any, liable to be recovered 
from the Tea Company, keeping in view the polluter 
pays principle, the precautionary  principle and the 
principle of restitution of the damaged ecosystem. 
The CEC shall also examine whether any residual or 
continuing environmental risk remains in the areas 
formerly under the tea plantation  and make specific 
recommendations regarding remediation, restoration 
and long-term ecological monitoring, together with a 
reasoned assessment of the quantum and manner of 
recovery of the  environmental 
compensation/compensatory fine from the Tea 
Company. 
 

## Page 145

20 
 
30. The CEC shall submit its report on the BBTCL 
aspect upon completion of the aforesaid exercise. 
31. Shri Jaideep Gupta, learned senior counsel 
appearing for the State of Tamil Nadu, seeks two 
weeks’ time to file a response to the CEC Report. Time 
as prayed for is granted. The State of Tamil Nadu 
shall file its reply within a period of two weeks.  
32. The reply shall, in particular, disclose the 
following: 
i. The nature, extent and present status of silk 
cotton cultivation within the Reserved Forest 
area, including the extent of land under such 
cultivation, the persons/entities undertaking or 
facilitating such cultivation, and the material 
available with the State regarding the 
involvement of persons from outside the area; 
ii. Complete particulars of the pattas granted by the 
District Collector in respect of lands falling 
within the area in question, including the date of 
grant, the authority under which the pattas were 
granted, the survey numbers and extent of land 
covered thereby, and the legal 
status/classification of such land on the date of 
grant; 

## Page 146

21 
 
iii. The person -wise status of all 118 Government 
servants identified as encroachers, including 
whether notice has been issued and served upon 
each of them and, in cases where notice has not 
been served, the specific reasons for non-service, 
along with the status of disciplinary proceedings 
and action for removal of their encroachments; 
and 
iv. The status of the claims under the Forest Rights 
Act, 2006, including the number of claims 
already determined and the forest rights 
recognised and pattas granted thereunder, as 
also the number and present stage of the claims 
which remain pending. 
33. List the matters as part-heard on 8th September, 
2026 for further hearing and consideration.

                             O R D E R
 Heard learned Senior Counsel/Counsel for the parties.
2. At the outset, Mr. Jayant Mehta, learned Senior Counsel
representing  the  Respondent  No.99  (Manipal  Cigna  Health
Insurance) submits that Mr. Joydeep Saha, Managing Director and
Chief Executive Officer of the Insurance Company has been
called today as there was some miscommunication with regard to
him filing an affidavit. He submits that he is present and has
filed his personal affidavit. Thus, personal presence of Mr.
Joydeep Saha is dispensed with, for the present. 
3. The matter started on an innocuous issue of whether a
vehicle which was said to be the cause of an accident, was the
real vehicle involved in the said accident. But as the events
8

## Page 174

SLP (C) NO.5582/2023
unfolded, an exercise has been taken pan India, pursuant to the
order of this Court in the present proceedings to unearth
whether fraudulent claims are being filed, that too, in a fixed
pattern, where the same vehicle is shown to be involved in
multiple accidents, which results in such frivolous claims
being  allowed.  This  appeared  to  be  a  fraud  of  enormous
proportion and has persuaded the Court to enlarge the scope of
the present proceedings to unravel and also to check such
fraudulent claims, which ultimately result in not only undue
financial stress on the Insurance Companies, but also on the
system and one of the fallouts is that the common genuine
consumer  has  to  pay  a  higher  premium,  just  because  the
Insurance companies have to ensure their financial viability. 
4. At this juncture, we called upon Mr. Jagdish Chandra
Solanki, learned counsel to assist the Court on various issues
as he has experience in these matters, and has also had the
privilege of working in an Insurance Company, where, according
to  him,  he  came  across  various  irregularities,  acts  of
commission/omission  and  lack  of  oversight,  which  had
facilitated the frauds to perpetuate. He has suggested that the
Court may implead the Insurance Regulatory and Development
Authority (IRDA) under the Ministry of Finance, Government of
India, as a party respondent, as all the Insurance Companies
ultimately are governed by the regulations made by IRDA. He
further submitted that a common portal be developed where all
9

## Page 175

SLP (C) NO.5582/2023
insurance claims be shown so that there can be ready access by
all the Insurance Companies with regard to any claim which may
be filed, so as to cross check the records of the other
companies as to whether such vehicle/person/institution/entity
is involved in repeated and multiple claims being made on a
regular basis. He submits that as of now two portals, i.e.,
VAHAN and SARATHI are available, which basically cater to data
collection and the submission is that if they can also be
integrated with the common portal, there can be ease of
tracking all such claims, both with regard to the veracity of
the accident, if any, the vehicle involved and the exact place
where the accident has occurred.  
5. A suggestion has also been made by Ms. Rupali Samuel,
learned Standing Counsel for the State of Tamil Nadu that the
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, Government of India
has a portal named E-detailed Accident Report (EDAR), which
tracks accidents on the National Highways across India. It was
submitted that if the same can be integrated with the other
portals which carry such data as also with the portal of the
IRDA,  the  authenticity  and  correctness  of  the  accident
occurring and the vehicle involved can be addressed more
readily and conveniently. 
6. Learned counsel for the State of Uttar Pradesh submits that
a special SIT was constituted for the purposes of verification
of these claims relating to complaints being received by the
10

## Page 176

SLP (C) NO.5582/2023
insurance companies indicating potential frauds, was pursuant
to the orders passed by a Coordinate Bench of this Court in
SLP(Civil) No.1110/2017 titled “Safiq  Ahmad  vs.  ICICI  Lombard
General  Insurance  Co.  Ltd.  &  Ors. ”. She submits that till
recently,  2188  complaints  were  received,  in  which,  upon
inquiry, over 1029 were investigated and 231 FIRs have been
lodged against 533 accused persons. We appreciate the action
taken by the State of Uttar Pradesh in the matter. We are
informed  that  other  States  might  have  also  followed  the
procedure. However, for the present, we are not going into that
individually. 
7. A fresh direction is issued to all the States to constitute
a special dedicated SIT for such purposes at the State level.
All complaints by the Insurance Companies be forwarded to the
said body, which will be looked into expeditiously. The States
are directed to provide sufficient hands to the SIT for
completion  of  the  investigations.  The  States  should  also
disclose with regard to the procedure they have adopted for
investigating in the present matter. 
8. At this point, the Court deems it appropriate to indicate
that it shall be the responsibility of the Insurance Companies
that all claims indicative of fraud are forwarded to the SIT
and pick and choose approach is not done. The Court will hold
the top most management of the concerned Insurance Companies
accountable if it is found that there has been selective
11

## Page 177

SLP (C) NO.5582/2023
forwarding of the cases to the SIT of the concerned State. Any
recommendation by the SIT or FIR lodged against the officers of
the Insurance Companies shall also be taken cognizance of and
appropriate action on the departmental side shall also be
initiated against such officials by the concerned Insurance
Companies, without any delay. 
9. The Insurance Companies shall file their affidavits as to
what action has been taken by them in terms of what has been
indicated hereinabove, both with regard to the cases referred
to the SIT, as also the in-house action taken against the
officials, who may play a role prejudicial to the interest of
the Company and facilitated the fraud which was attempted or
committed by the parties concerned.
10. Let the IRDA be impleaded as respondent no.104. Similarly,
the Ministry of Finance, though the Secretary, Union of India
be impleaded as respondent no. 105; the Ministry of Road
Transport and Highways through the Secretary be impleaded as
respondent no.106; the General Insurance Council (GIC), which
we are informed is the overall body under the IRDA which is
responsible for coordinating among the Insurance Companies and
also  laying  down  general  policies,  be  also  impleaded  as
respondent no.107.
11. Notices shall be sent to the newly added respondents by the
Registry forthwith and they shall also file their affidavits
giving details of what is their responsibility at present, how
12

## Page 178

SLP (C) NO.5582/2023
they discharge the same and what, according to them, could be
the steps which are required to be taken, meaning thereby that
they shall give their suggestions how to handle or take care of
the  situation,  which  the  Court  is  taking  note  of  and
considering in the present proceedings.  
12. The matters be listed on 23.09.2026 at 2.00 p.m.
13. On the next date, learned counsel for all the parties
should be ready with a one page note which would be a
precis/summary  of  their  affidavits  for  the  Court’s  ready
reference. 
14. After the order was dictated, a suggestion has come from
Mr. Solanki, learned counsel, that wherever the Insurance claim
is  negated  by  the  concerned  MACT  on  the  ground  of
fraud/collusion, the concerned Insurance Company would carry
out an in-house appraisal of the said case and also forward
details of the same to the SIT of the concerned State in which
the incident has occurred, for action. We find the suggestion
to be useful and relevant. Accordingly, a direction is issued
to the Insurance Companies that such matters where the claim is
negated on the ground of fraud or collusion, the said Insurance
Company shall immediately forward the details of the said case
to the SIT of the State where the claim is raised and also
carry out an in-house investigation with regard to whether
there was contributory collusion by its officers.
15. Details  of  the  same  shall  also  be  disclosed  in  the
13

## Page 179

SLP (C) NO.5582/2023
affidavits to be filed by all concerned. 
16. At this juncture, we reiterate that in our order dated
18.03.2026 at paragraph no.7 we had indicated that all the
respondents may take note of the action taken by the State of
Odisha pursuant to the directions of this Court in the present
proceedings and accordingly, come up with their own modalities.
17. The CMD of the following Insurance companies were required
to be present physically today before this Court in terms of
Paragraph No.5 of order dated 26.05.2026, as they had not
entered appearance pursuant to the directions of this Court
issued vide order dated 06.04.2026:

18. Mr.  Krishnan  Ramachandran,  Chairman,  Respondent  No.100
14

## Page 180

SLP (C) NO.5582/2023
(Niva Bupa Health Insurance Co. Ltd.) has appeared through
virtual mode, as also the CMDs of Respondent No. 79 (Liberty
General Insurance Limited) and Respondent No. 93 ( Zuno General
Insurance Ltd), which was not the liberty given to the Parties
vide order dated 26.05.2026.  
19. Though we were of the opinion that notice for contempt be
issued and they be directed to appear before this Court on the
next date of listing along with their show cause, but by way of
extraordinary indulgence, we refrain from doing so, for the
present. Thus, notice is issued against all the CMDs of the
Insurance Companies mentioned in paragraph No.17 above to show
cause, by filing a personally affirmed affidavit, as to why
they have not complied with the directions of this Court to be
physically  present  before  this  Court  today  in  terms  of
directions issued vide order dated 26.05.2026. 
20. We further note here that Affidavits have been filed by all
the Insurance Companies except respondents No. 64, 94 and 98.
They have neither entered appearance, nor filed affidavit.
21. In  view  of  service  of  notice  not  being  complete  on
respondent No.53, Sahara India Life Insurance Company, let
fresh notice be issued.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The matter has come up today to report compliance of our
directions issued in the Judgment titled “Yash Charitable & Ors.
vs. Union of India & Ors. ” (Writ Petition (Civil) No.369/2022
decided on 30-1-2026).
2. We take notice of the fact that a short affidavit has been
filed on behalf of the Department of Health Research, Ministry of
Health and Family Welfare, duly affirmed by its Director Shri
Murari Lal Sharma. This affidavit only talks about the direction
and its compliance issued by this Court as contained in Para 153 of
the main Judgment.
3. According to Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, the learned Additional
Solicitor General, Union in its Ministry of Health needs to file a
comprehensive and detailed compliance report insofar as all other
directions are concerned. 
4. We grant four weeks time to the Ministry of Health to file a
detailed  Status  Report  on  all  aspects  of  the  matter,  more
particularly, highlighting in what manner Union has looked into the
Judgment and in what manner it intends to implement all the

## Page 184

4
directions issued and what have been done so far.
5. At this stage, we must also take notice of one Interlocutory
Application preferred by the Respondent No.9 namely Neurogen Brain
and Spine Institute Pvt. Ltd. This Institute has many suggestions
to put forward. 
6. We request Ms. Bhati to look into the IA filed by the
Respondent No.9 along with the materials  attached with the IA.
Perhaps some of their suggestions may be helpful to the Union in
effective and meaningful implementation of the various directions
issued by this Court. If the Union has constituted any Expert Body
for this purpose, the suggestions put forward along with the other
materials in the IA may also be looked into.
7. Mr. Shyam Divan, the learned Senior counsel has also appeared
today in one of the Interlocutory Applications preferred by  the
Parents Forum for Stem Cells in Autism and Cerebral Palsy, the
original Respondent No.13.
8. According to Mr. Divan, he represents all those parents whose
children as on date are undergoing the stem cell therapy treatment
for autism. However, Mr. Divan would like to wait till the Union
files an exhaustive report as referred to above.
9. We shall look into the IA preferred by the Respondent No.13 on
the next date of hearing.
10. Post this matter for further hearing on 1-9-2026.
Writ Petition (Civil) No.731/2026:-
1. This matter came up for hearing before the Bench during the
partial Court working days. 
2. On 12-6-2026, the following Order was passed:-
“Upon  hearing  learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
petitioner,  we  find  that  the  impugned  letters  dated
10.03.2026,  11.03.2026  and  the  impugned  advisory  dated
25.03.2026 have been issued in compliance of the order passed
by this Court in the matter bearing Writ Petition (C) No. 369
of 2022, titled “Yash Charitable Trust & Ors. Vs. Union of
India  &  Ors.”  and  the  said  matter  is  still  pending
consideration before this Court.
In view of the above, tag this Writ Petition with W.P. (C)
No. 369 of 2022. 

## Page 185

5
However, the directions issued by this Court in W.P. (C) No.
369 of 2022 should be complied with.”
3. In the Writ Petition preferred by the Society of Regenerative
Sciences, the following reliefs have been prayed for:-
i. “Issue a writ of certiorari or a writ in the nature of
certiorari, or any other appropriate writ, order direction,
quashing and setting aside the Impugned Letter bearing D.O. No.
M-11019/5/2026-CG dated 10 March 2026 issued by the Respondent
No.4/DG-ICMR
ii. Issue a writ of certiorari or a writ in the nature of
certiorari, or any other appropriate writ, order direction,
quashing  and  setting  aside  the  Impugned  Letter-II  dated
11019/5/2026-CG) 11 March 2026 (File No. M- No.4 issued by
Respondent (Department of Health Research) through the NECRBHR;
iii. Issue a writ of certiorari or a writ in the nature of
certiorari, or any other appropriate writ, order direction,
quashing and setting aside the Impugned Advisory dated 25.03.2026
issued by Respondent No.2 (National Medical Commission);
iv. Issue a writ of mandamus or a writ in the nature of mandamus,
or any other appropriate writ, order or direction, declaring that
ACP involving minimum manipulation, carried out by Registered
Medical Practitioners in a single sitting for the treatment of
their own patients and not for commercialisation outside their
clinics or hospitals, fall outside the purview of the Drugs and
Cosmetics Act, 1940 and it is inappropriate to intervene from
regulatory angle on routine practices/ therapies/ surgeries/
transplantations undertaken by Registered Medical Practitioners/
physicians / doctors in their clinics/hospitals involving such
cell procedures for the treatment of their patients based on
their medical expertise and the New Drugs and Clinical Trials
Rules, 2019, in terms of the statutory clarification dated 09
February 2021 under Section 33P of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act,
1940, read with the recommendations of the Drugs Technical
Advisory  Board  in  its  84th  Meeting  dated  27  August  2019;
v. Issue a writ of mandamus or a writ in the nature of mandamus,
or any other appropriate writ, order or direction, declaring that
Respondent No.s 2, 3 and 4 have no or statutory mandate,
legislative competence delegated authority to regulate, restrict,
prohibit or declare as "illegal" the clinical practice of ACP by
Registered Medical Practitioners in India;
vi Issue a writ of and in the nature of mandamus or other orders
or  directions  to  Respondent  No.1  to  constitute  an  expert
committee to look into and examine the functioning and affairs of
Respondent Nos.2-4, with respect to the nexus with private
companies  manufacturing  Stem  Cell  Derived  Products;
vii. To set up an expert committee formed by the Hon'ble Court to
evaluate scientific publications in this field with right of

## Page 186

6
hearing  to  be  granted  to  the  main  stakeholders,  including
patients suffering from incurable conditions who have benefitted
from autologous cell procedure as well as representatives of the
Petitioner  Society  who  administer  such  procedures  to  such
patients;
viii. Pending hearing and final disposal of the present Writ
Petition, be pleased to stay the operation, implementation and
enforcement of the Impugned Letter dated 10 March 2026, the
Impugned Letter-II dated 11 March 2026, and the Impugned Advisory
dated  25.03.2026,  and  further  direct  that  no  coercive  or
disciplinary action shall be taken against any Registered Medical
Practitioner or any member of the Petitioner society pursuant to
the said Impugned Communications;
ix. Pass such further and other orders / directions as this
Hon'ble Court may deem just, fit and proper in the facts and
circumstances of the case and in the interests of justice.”
4. We hard Mr. Nalin Kohli, the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the petitioner.
5. What we have been able to understand is that the Medical
Council of India has issued some advisories keeping in mind the
Judgment delivered by this Court in “Yash Charitable & Ors. vs.
Union of India & Ors.”. The petitioner seeks to challenge the
legality and validity of the advisories. These advisories may be
based on the Judgment but as such has no direct connection with the
Judgment delivered by us.
6. Although the Bench during the partial Court working days
ordered  that  the  petition  be  tagged  with  Writ  Petition  (C)
No.369/2022, yet we want the Registry to place this petition before
Hon’ble Chief Justice of India and obtain appropriate orders.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
TRANSFER PETITION No.2608/2025
KEERTHI L ..... PETITIONER(S)
              VERSUS
MANJUNATHA M S ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. We have heard learned counsel for the parties. We have also
interacted with the petitioner-wife and the respondent-husband.
2. Petitioner and respondent entered into wedlock on 27.05.2011
and solemnized their marriage as per Hindu rites and customs.
Additionally, the marriage was also registered before the Registrar
of  Marriages,  Byatarayanapura,  Bengaluru  on  30.05.2011.  On
12.03.2020, petitioner-wife gave birth to twin babies, both of them
are now about 6 years old.
3. Unfortunately, matrimonial dispute and discord arose between
the parties which led to the petitioner-wife filing a petition for
divorce under Section 13(1)(ia) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
before the Principal Family Judge at Bengaluru, Karnataka, which
was registered as MC No.524 of 2025. At that stage, petitioner by
virtue of her employment was residing at Bengaluru.
4. Petitioner is an Assistant Director in the Ministry of Home
Affairs, Government of India. In connection with her employment,
she  was  transferred  to  New  Delhi  whereafter  she  joined  her
transferred post at New Delhi on 04.08.2025. 
1

## Page 205

5. In such circumstances, petitioner filed the present Transfer
Petition seeking transfer of proceedings from Bengaluru to New
Delhi.
6. Learned Chamber Judge after noticing that there were chances
of amicable settlement of the matrimonial dispute between the
parties, referred the matter to the Supreme Court Mediation Centre.
Due to the sincere efforts of the learned Mediator and the
conciliatory approach of the contesting parties, they could arrive
at a settlement agreement dated 25.05.2026.
7. Thereafter, both petitioner and the respondent have filed a
joint application under Article 142 of the Constitution of India
seeking  dissolution  of  marriage  in  terms  of  the  settlement
agreement dated 25.05.2026. Relevant portion of the settlement
agreement is extracted hereunder:
9.  NOW  THEREFORE  THIS  SETTLEMENT  AGREEMENT
WITNESSETH AS UNDER:
A.  The  Parties  hereto  mutually  agree  that
despite their best efforts, they are unable to
continue their relationship of husband and wife
owing to personal differences.
B.  Both Parties further agree that they do not
hold  either  of  the  other  party  or  their
respective family members responsible for the
breakdown of their relationship.
C. The Petitioner confirms that the Respondent
has returned all her belongings and articles,
including  jewellery,  ornaments,  stridhan,
clothes and other personal belongings and there
is no subsisting dispute between the parties
towards exchange/return of any such articles.
D.  Both  the  parties  agree  that  they  are
2

## Page 206

financially  independent,  self-sufficient  to
lead their independent life. The Petitioner
further agrees waives all her rights and claim
towards permanent alimony and maintenance. The
Petitioner further waives all her right in
respect of the money earned by the Petitioner
and  invested  in  the  Family  during  the
subsistence of the marriage i.e. from the date
of marriage till the date of separation of the
parties, for the purpose of this settlement.
The Petitioner shall henceforth have no claim
against the Respondent or any of his family
members whether civil or criminal including
future maintenance or claim any rights over any
of the property of the Respondent and his
family members under any provision of law.
E.  The  Respondent  shall  pay  the  monthly
maintenance of a sum of Rs. 10,000/- (Rupees
Ten Thousand only) per month each to the two
girl children towards their maintenance. The
Respondent  shall  deposit  the  said  monthly
maintenance in the respective Bank Accounts of
the two girl children. It is further agreed
between the parties that the Respondent shall
increase the monthly maintenance at the rate of
10% per annum and continue to remit the same in
the respective bank accounts of the minors till
they  attain  self-sufficient  and  well
established. It is further clarified that the
present  settlement  shall  not  affect  the
statutory  right  of  the  minor  daughters  in
succession of the properties. Further, if the
daughters choose to assert or claim their right
in  the  future,  they  shall  be  entitled  to
exercise all legal rights of succession in the
3

## Page 207

properties of the Respondent.
F. It is further agreed between the parties
that the custody of both the minor Child remain
with the Petitioner till their age of majority
and thereafter they are free to move with their
parents as per their wish. Till the both the
minor child attain the age of Majority, the
Respondent is entitled to visit the Children
for two days in a year (preferably one day in
Summer and one day in Winter Vacations) in a
place chosen by the Petitioner for minimum 3 to
8 hours subject to the comfort and convenience
of the children. The details of the date, place
of  meeting  shall  be  communicated  by  the
Petitioner  to  the  Respondent  15  days  in
advance. The Respondent is also entitled to do
a whatsapp video call with his children on 1st
Sunday of every month at 11.00 AM. in the
Whatsapp  Number  of  the  Petitioner  i.e
9916991233.
G. It is further agreed between the parties
that in the event of any medical emergency to
the Children the Petitioner agrees to inform
the Respondent immediately and the Respondent
is entitled to visit their children in those
circumstances, subject to the condition that
the  Respondent  taking  care  of  all  medical
expenses of such emergency.
H.  The permanent custody/guardianship of both
the  minor  daughters  shall  remain  with
Petitioner and she will be upbringing them.
Petitioner will decide the matters related to
education, health and overall welfare of both
the minor daughters.
I. The parties further agree that in view of
4

## Page 208

the settlement recorded in this agreement, the
parties  shall  jointly  move  an  Application
before the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India under
Article 142 of the Constitution of India for
grant of decree of divorce and dissolution of
marriage and for closing/quashing of all the
complaints/petitions/suits  filed  by  the
Petitioner and the Respondent respectively.
J. The Petitioner and the Respondent hereby
undertakes to make a joint Application before
the Hon'ble Supreme Court for disposal of the
above Transfer Petition (Civil) No. 2608 of
2025 pending before this Hon'ble Court in terms
of this settlement agreement in the following
manner:
a. Pass a decree of divorce by dissolving the
marriage solemnized on 27.5.2011 between the

8. In the course of the hearing, we have drawn the attention of
the  respondent-husband  to  the  terms  of  visitation  rights  as
provided for in Clause F of the settlement agreement, as extracted
supra, and whether he is agreeable to such limited visitation
rights. On our query, he submits that he is satisfied with the
visitation rights provided for in Clause F. Since, we are dealing
with human lives and the relationship of parents with their
children, we leave it open to the parties if they feel that the
visitation rights of the respondent needs enlargement, it will
always be open to the parties to approach the court for relaxation
of the conditions in Clause F. 
9. Consequently and in view of the settlement, the marriage
between the petitioner and the respondent is hereby dissolved.

O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. Leave granted.
3. The  present  appeals  arise  out  of  a  common  order  dated
11.12.2024 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Patna in CRADB
No(s).1136, 1150, 1181, 1238 and 1278 of 2024, by which the private
respondents have been granted the benefit of suspension of sentence
and release on bail during the pendency of their appeals.
4. The private respondents stood convicted for the offences under
Sections 302/34 read with Section 120(B) of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 (for short “IPC”) and 27(3) of the Arms Act, 1959 (for short
“Arms Act”) and were sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life and
to pay a fine of Rs. 10,000/- (Rupees Ten Thousand) each under
Section 302/34 read with Section 120B of the IPC . Sunil Kumar
(private respondent No.1 in  SLP (Crl.) No.2129 of 2025)  Crwas
further sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life and to pay a
fine of Rs.10,000/- (Rupees Ten Thousand) under Section 27(3) of
the Arms Act and in default of payment of fine, to further suffer
S.I. for three months. 
5. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  submitted  that  the
appellant's  husband  was  brutally  killed  and  the  same  is
corroborated by the postmortem report, inasmuch as wounds were

## Page 218

5
found on his body. It was submitted that the High Court, without
considering that the private respondents’ conviction was based on
cogent consideration of the evidence adduced during trial and also
on reasoning which could sustain the test of law to connect the
private respondents to the crime, has in a very casual manner
allowed their prayer for suspension of sentence and release on bail
during the pendency of their appeals. It was submitted that the
respondents  had  not  even  completed  three  years  of  actual
incarceration. It was contended that the ground which has appealed
to the High Court was a very specious ground, i.e., the Doctor who
conducted the postmortem had admitted that it was his first such
case and that he was not very well versed with forensic science.
6. It was further contended that another ground which has found
favour with the Court was that though the informant is not a
Pardanashin lady and was the Mukhiya of the Gram Panchayat at the
relevant point of time, the FIR was still not lodged promptly by
her and there was a delay of 48 hours, which lent credibility to
the defence story that there was false implication because of
political motives. It was contended that in the background of these
facts, and considering that some of the private respondents have a
chequered history of numerous criminal antecedents, that too under
serious sections of the relevant penal codes, the decision needed
interference.
7. Learned counsel for the private respondents have individually
addressed the Court. The common thread of argument was that the
High Court has taken a holistic view and has appreciated the basic
infirmity in the prosecution case with regard to delay and also

## Page 219

6
with regard to the reliability of the forensic findings in the
postmortem report. It was contended that some of the respondents
concerned, though having criminal antecedents, are on bail in all
other cases. However, they could not defend the order of the High
Court impugned with regard to the reasoning given by the Court
while allowing the prayer for suspension of sentence and release of
the private respondents on bail.
8. Having considered the matter in its entirety and going through
the material on record, we find force in the submissions of the
learned counsel for the appellants. The order of the Trial Court
cannot be doubted so casually on a sketchy consideration and
misplaced reliance on the isolated fact that the delay in reporting
the matter was by the wife who was a sitting Mukhiya,  as has been
observed by the High Court and being the sole ground for allowing
the prayer for suspension of the sentence awarded by the Trial
Court.
9. The discussion relating to the statement of the witnesses, the
relationship of the accused among themselves and the recovery of
the material objects used in the crime, has been dealt with by the
Trial Court, which could not be said to be perverse. However, we
refrain from going further on merits, as ultimately the appeals
pending before the High Court have to be heard on merits.
10. For the reasons aforesaid, the appeals are allowed. The order
granting suspension of sentence and grant of bail to the private
respondents stands set aside. They are directed to surrender before
the Trial Court within two weeks from today, whereupon they shall
be taken into judicial custody.

## Page 220

7
11. However, it shall always be open to the respondents to move
before the High Court for early disposal of their appeals. Further,
any observation made in the present appeals, being solely for the
purposes of considering the matter with regard to suspension of
sentence and the release of the private respondents on bail, shall
not cause any prejudice to the private respondents while hearing
their substantive appeals.
12. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

   UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. In compliance of our order dated 03.02.2026, Mr. Manish Kumar,
learned  standing  counsel  for  the  State  of  Bihar,  has  taken
instructions.
2. Having considered the matter in detail, we are of the opinion
that 1362 candidates, including the intervenors, who are present
before this Court, must be appointed to the post of Auxiliary Nurse
and Midwife.
3. Before completing the process, we are of the opinion that the
State Government can process their candidature by considering

## Page 232

9
whether they possess the requisite qualifications or not. For this
purpose, State Government may constitute a two-member Committee for
verification and examination. The whole process shall be completed
within one month from today. Learned counsels appearing for the
candidates  agree  that  the  candidates  will  appear  before  the
Committee between 07.09.2026 to 12.09.2026 as intimated to them in
advance. 
4. Mr. Manish Kumar will take instructions to report about the
completion of the process by next date of hearing.
5. List on 13.10.2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.7454 of 2026)
MANOJ BHIMRAO CHAUDHANTE APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The  present  appellant  -  Manoj  Bhimrao
Chaudhante,  would  assail  his  conviction  and
sentence by the Trial Court and the High Court
concurrently,  for  committing  offense  under
Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for
short ‘IPC’) for committing murder of deceased
Vicky at around 03:00 PM on 14.04.2014. 
3. As a matter of fact, six accused persons,
namely appellant Manoj (Accused No.1), Sachin
(Accused No.2), Ankush (Accused No.3), Bhimrao
(Accused No.4), Arunabai (Accused No.5) and Rahul
1

## Page 243

(Accused No.6) were tried for committing offenses
under Sections 143, 147, 148, 302, 325, 323, 504
read with 149 IPC, under Section 135 Bombay
Police Act and under Section 4/25 of the Arms
Act.
4. While  the  appellant  and  Sachin  (Accused
No.2) have been convicted separately for offenses
under Sections 302 and 324 IPC respectively, the
other accused persons have been acquitted of all
the  charges.  All  the  accused  persons  were
acquitted for charges under Sections 143, 147,
148, 325, 323, 504 read with Section 149 IPC, and
under Section 135 of the Bombay Police Act and
4/25 of the Arms Act.
5. The prosecution case in a nutshell is that
Siddharth  Gajbhare  (PW-7)  was  appointed  as
President  of  the  Committee  to  celebrate  Dr.
Babasaheb  Ambedkar  Jayanti  at  Govind  Nagar,
Nanded. Accused Arunabai and Bhimrao, who are
parents of the appellant, were upset and annoyed
due to such appointment of Siddharth Gajbhare
(PW-7), and during the celebration at 12:00 noon,
the first incident took place, wherein, Siddharth
Gajbhare (PW-7) unplugged the music system (DJ)
and  therefore,  accused  Bhimrao  and  Arunabai
allegedly abused him.
2

## Page 244

6. In the afternoon around 3:00 PM, all the
accused persons came to the place of occurrence,
and appellant assaulted Vicky by means of knife
(single assault), whereas Sachin (Accused No.2)
assaulted Siddharth Gajbhare (PW-7) also with
knife on the left side of the waist. At such
time, other accused Ankush (Accused No.3), Love
and  Balu,  also  assaulted  younger  brother  of
Siddharth Gajbhare (PW-7), namely Gautam, with
stick, whereas sister of Siddharth Gajbhare (PW-
7) was also assaulted by means of fists and
slaps. While taken to hospital, the deceased
was declared brought dead.
7. Since the basic prosecution case and the
investigation is not disputed, and for the nature
of the order we propose to pass in this appeal,
we are skipping the narration about the steps
taken during investigation and the deposition of
entire prosecution witnesses. In this appeal,
this  Court  has  issued  notice  on  16.04.2026,
noting the submission of learned counsel for the
appellant, limiting to the quantum of sentence,
by submitting that the offense would fall under
3

## Page 245

Section 304 Part-I or Part-II of the IPC, rather
than Section 302 IPC.
8. Having  heard  learned  counsel  for  the
parties, we are inclined to accept and hold that
the present offense would fall under Section 304
Part-I IPC for the reasons given hereinafter.
9. The first incident took place around 12:00
noon, wherein the appellant did not participate.
It was only his parents, namely Bhimrao (Accused
No.4) and Arunabai (Accused No.5), who abused
Siddharth Gajbhare (PW-7). Although, it is the
prosecution case that all of them again reached
the place of occurrence around 3:00 PM and the
appellant and Sachin (Accused No.2) were armed
with knife, the fact remains that there is no
separate charge of conspiracy either alleged in
the charge sheet or tried by the Trial Court.
10. Moreover,  the  charge  of  sharing  common
intention by all the six accused persons under
Section 149 IPC has also found not been proved by
the Trial Court, as all the accused persons have
been acquitted of the charges under Sections 143,
147, 148, and 149 IPC. Thus, at present, it is
not the case that the appellant was sharing
common  intention  with  other  accused  persons,
4

## Page 246

having reached the place of occurrence in a
premeditated  state  of  mind  by  conspiring  to
commit murder of deceased Vicky.
11. The earlier incident may be the root cause
for occurrence of the second incident, which
eventually  resulted  in  the  murder  of  Vicky,
however, the fact remains that the appellant has
given a single blow to the deceased. It is also
to be noted that the entire occurrence had its
genesis  in  the  celebration  of  Dr.  Babasaheb
Ambedkar Jayanti, wherein Siddharth Gajbhare (PW-
7) was appointed as President of the organizing
Committee, which was not liked by the appellant’s
parents. Thus, as per the prosecution case, it is
not  the  appellant  who  had  a  grudge  against
Siddharth Gajbhare (PW-7) in the beginning, but
it was his parents who were having a grudge, who
participated in the first incident.
12. It is also to be noted that the parents of
the  appellant  who  participated  in  the  first
incident have been acquitted in the present case,
and as such, the basic case of the prosecution is
not that the appellant had any intention to
commit murder of Vicky from the very beginning,
otherwise the Trial Court would have convicted
all  the  accused  persons  for  sharing  common
5

## Page 247

intention.
13. In view of the above, we hold that the
appellant had intention to assault the deceased
by giving a single stab wound, however, he had no
knowledge that the assault caused by him would
result in the deceased's death. Thus, considering
all the above features of the case, we hold that
the appellant has committed an offense under
Section 304 Part-I IPC and not under Section 302
IPC.
14. Accordingly, we allow the appeal in part,
set aside appellant's conviction under Section
302 IPC, and instead convict him for committing
offense under Section 304 Part-I IPC.
15. The appellant has already undergone sentence
of more than 10 years (around 10 years 6 months).
This Court would therefore impose sentence to the
appellant to the period already undergone.
16. The appellant be released from jail, if he
is not required in any other offense. Bail bonds
stand discharged.
6

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No. 3772 OF 2026
PREM CHAND PAL @ PREM CHANDRA PAL ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF JHARKHAND ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. By the impugned order dated 26.08.2025, the High Court of
Jharkhand at Ranchi (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter) rejected
the  interlocutory  application  filed  by  the  appellant  seeking
exemption from surrendering. Further, the High Court directed that
within 6 weeks’ time if the appellant did not surrender and produce
the surrender certificate before the High Court, the Criminal
Revision Petition would stand dismissed.
4. Be it stated that appellant was prosecuted under Sections 420,
467, 471 and 474 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’).
The  Trial  Court  convicted  the  appellant  under  the  aforesaid
provisions and sentenced him to undergo Rigorous Imprisonment (RI)
for 3 years and fine of 3,000/- with a default stipulation.₹
5. On appeal, the appellate Court acquitted the appellant under
Section 420 IPC but the conviction under Sections 467, 468, 471 and
474 of IPC was maintained; so also the sentence of RI for 3 years
and fine. 
6. Aggrieved by the aforesaid order of the Appellate Court,
1

## Page 252

appellant preferred a criminal revision before the High Court,
being  Criminal  Revision  No.285/2024.  Along  with  the  criminal
revision, appellant also filed an interlocutory application for
grant of exemption from surrendering. By the impugned order, the
High Court relied upon Rule 159 of the Jharkhand High Court Rules,
2001 and held that in view of the express language of the aforesaid
provision, the prayer for exemption from surrendering could not be
entertained. Consequently, the interlocutory application seeking
exemption from surrendering has been dismissed with consequential
direction to the appellant to surrender and to submit surrender
certificate for considering the criminal revision on merit.
7. Learned Chamber Judge vide order dated 05.01.2026, considered
the nature of sentence imposed upon the appellant whereafter
exemption was granted from surrendering till the first date of
listing  before  the  Court.  Thereafter,  notice  was  issued  on
16.01.2026 and in the subsequent order dated 14.07.2026, the order
granting exemption has been directed to be continued until further
orders.
8. Rule 159 of the Jharkhand High Court Rules, 2001 reads thus:
“159. In the case of revision under Sections
397  and  401  of  the  Code  of  Criminal
Procedure, 1973, arising out of conviction
and sentence of imprisonment, the petitioner
shall state whether the petition shall be
accompanied  by  a  certified  copy  of  the
relevant order. If he has not surrendered the
petition  shall  he  accompanied  by  an
application seeking leave to surrender within
a specified period. On sufficient cause being
2

## Page 253

shown, the Bench may grant such time and, on
such conditions, as it thinks fit and proper.
No  such  revision  shall  be  posted  for
admission  unless  the  petitioner  has
surrendered  to  custody  in  the  concerned
Court”.
9. A perusal of the aforesaid provision could go to show that if
the revision petitioner has not surrendered in terms of his
conviction  and  sentence  of  imprisonment,  he  shall  file  an
application seeking leave to surrender within a specified period
and on sufficient cause being shown, the Bench may grant such time
on such conditions as it thinks fit and proper. However, it is
provided that no revision shall be posted for admission unless
revision petitioner has surrendered to custody in the concerned
court. 
10. Validity of Rule 159 of the Jharkhand High Court Rules, 2001
was questioned before this Court in Vivek Rai And Another vs. High
Court of Jharkhand,  (2015) 12 SCC 86. A Two-Judge Bench of this
Court rejected the challenge on the ground that when a person is
convicted by two courts, he shall obey the law and should not
abscond. Such a provision cannot be held to be arbitrary. Relevant
portion of the judgment in Vivek Rai is extracted hereunder:
6. We do not find any merit in the challenge
to the validity of the Rule. It is well-known
practice that generally a revision against
conviction and sentence is filed after an
appeal is dismissed and the convicted person
is taken into custody in the Court itself.
The object of the Rule is to ensure that a
3

## Page 254

person who has been convicted by two courts
obeys the law and does not abscond. The
provision cannot thus be held to be arbitrary
in any manner. The provision is to regulate
the procedure of the Court and does not, in
any manner, conflict with the substantive
provisions  of  CrPC  relied  upon  by  the
petitioners.
11. However, the Bench observed that Rule 159 of the Jharkhand
High Court Rules, 2001 does not affect the inherent power of the
High Court to exempt the requirement of surrender in exceptional
situation. The Bench observed that if the Court grants exemption
from surrendering and directs listing of a case, Rule 159 cannot
stand in the way of the court’s exercise of inherent jurisdiction.
Para 11 of the judgment in Vivek Rai reads thus:
11. It has not been disputed even by the
learned counsel for the High Court that the
Rule does not affect the inherent power of
the High Court to exempt the requirement of
surrender  in  exceptional  situations.  It
cannot  thus,  be  argued  that  prohibition
against posting of a revision petition for
admission applies even to a situation where
on an application of the petitioner, on a
case being made out, the Court, in exercise
of  its  inherent  power,  considers  it
appropriate to grant exemption from surrender
having regard to the nature and circumstances
of a case. Thus, the exception as found in
the corresponding Supreme Court Rules that if
the Court grants exemption from surrender and
directs listing of a case, the Rule cannot
4

## Page 255

stand in the way of the Court's exercise of
such jurisdiction, has to be assumed in the
impugned Rule.
12. In  Daulat Singh Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh,  Special Leave
Petition (Criminal) Diary No.20900/2024, decided on 30.07.2024,
this Court expressed doubt about the correctness of the proposition
laid down in  Vivek Rai  observing that such a proposition is
debatable and that it would not be appropriate to accept it as a
sound proposition of law. Relevant portion of the decision in
Daulat Singh is extracted hereunder:
11. If indeed such observation has to be
construed as a proposition of law having been
laid down by this Court that a high court in
exercise  of  its  inherent  powers  may,  in
exceptional cases, exempt the requirement of
surrender, as learned counsel would wish us
to construe, we find such proposition to be
debatable. Inherent powers of a high court
saved by Section 482 of the Code of Criminal
Procedure are to be exercised  to make such
orders as may be necessary to give effect to
any order under the Code  (emphasis supplied
by us) or to prevent abuse of the process of
any court or otherwise to secure the ends of
justice. It could lead to a travesty of
justice if Section 482 of the Code were read
in a manner extending liberty to a convict to
urge a high court to exercise its inherent
power to grant exemption from surrender prior
to entertainment of a revision petition, when
there are concurrent findings rendered by two
courts of competent jurisdiction – conviction
5

## Page 256

recorded by  the trial court and affirmance
thereof  by  the  appellate  court  -  and
particularly when it is the duty of a high
court, even under Section 482, to give effect
to orders passed under the Code.
12.  Significantly,  the  legislature  having
thought  it  fit  to  introduce  a  provision
enabling  a  convict  to  seek  benefit  of
suspension of sentence pending an appeal did
so by enacting Section 389 of the Code. The
Code  has  no  provision  permitting  an
application to seek exemption from surrender.
We are minded to hold that the omission in
the Code with regard to providing an avenue
for a convict suffering a sentence to seek
exemption from surrender, pending a revision,
is a conscious act of the legislature.
13. We also find that there are specific
provisions in the Supreme Court Rules, 2013
providing for an application for exemption
from surrendering to be made, but similar
such provision is not otherwise available in
the 2008 Rules framed by the High Court.
14. It is a cardinal principle that while
gathering the legislative intent, attention
has to be paid to what has been said as well
as what has not been said.
15.  We  do  not,  therefore,  consider  it
appropriate to accept as a sound proposition
of law that a high court, in exercise of its
inherent  power,  may  grant  exemption  from
surrendering in a particular case despite
concurrent findings of conviction oblivious
of the duty of giving effect to orders passed
under the Code and/or to prevent abuse of the
6

## Page 257

process of a court.
16. Having regard to our disagreement with
the view expressed in Vivek Rai (supra),
which is a decision of a coordinate Bench,
reference to a larger Bench is desirable.
However,  notwithstanding  the  same  and
notwithstanding  the  finding  on
maintainability returned by the High Court,
we  have  looked  into  the  merits  of  the
petitioner’s claim; and, having regard to the
order we propose to pass, we do not consider
it necessary to make a reference.
13. Recently, a Two-Judge Bench of this Court in Sudhir Khaitan
vs. State of Rajasthan, Special Leave Petition Criminal Nos. 19025-
19027/2025, has referred the matter i.e., correctness of the
decision in Vivek Rai, to a larger Bench. 
14. We may also refer to Section 397 of the Code of Criminal
Procedure, 1973(CrPC) which deals with the exercise of the power of
revision by the High Court or by any Sessions Judge. As per sub-
section (1), the High Court or any Sessions Judge may call for and
examine the record of any proceeding before any inferior Criminal
Court situate within its or his local jurisdiction for the purpose
of satisfying itself or himself as to the correctness, legality or
propriety of any finding, sentence or order recorded or passed and
as to the regularity of any proceedings of such inferior Court. It
also provides that when calling for such record, the High Court or
the concerned Sessions Judge may direct that the execution of any
sentence  or  order  be  suspended  and  if  the  accused  is  in
confinement, that he be released on bail or on his own bond pending
7

## Page 258

the examination of the record. Thus, the CrPC itself enables the
High Court or any Sessions Court to suspend execution of any
sentence or order pending examination of the record which has been
called for to examine the correctness, legality or propriety of
such proceedings. 
15. However,  that  may  not  be  necessary.  Even  going  by  the
observations of the Two-Judge Bench in paragraph 11 of Vivek Rai,
we are of the view that having regard to the fact that the sentence
imposed upon the appellant is 3 years out of which he has already
undergone imprisonment of five and a half months, the present is a
fit case where exemption should be granted to the appellant from
surrendering and that custody of the revision petitioner should not
be insisted upon as a pre-condition for hearing of the criminal
revision petition. 
16. We, therefore, set aside the impugned order of the High Court
dated 26.08.2025 and make the order of the learned Chamber Judge
dated 05.01.2026 absolute. The High Court may now proceed to hear
Criminal Revision No.285/2024 on its own merit and in accordance
with law.
17. Appeal is accordingly allowed.
18.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
