O R D E R
1. A Joint Application being I.A. No.236265 of 2026 has
been filed seeking appropriate directions under Article
142 of the Constitution of India for dissolution of the
marriage between the parties by mutual consent, in terms
of the Settlement Agreement arrived at between them.
2. We appreciate the efforts taken by Ms.Yugandhara
Pawar Jha, learned Mediator, Supreme Court Mediation
Centre, who mediated the dispute between the parties. We
also appreciate the efforts put in by learned counsel
appearing for the parties.
3. Learned counsel appearing for the parties submit that
all disputes and differences between the parties have
been amicably resolved and that the parties have decided
to  part  ways  amicably  on  the  terms  and  conditions
contained in the Settlement Agreement dated 27.07.2026.
Accordingly, it is prayed that appropriate and necessary
orders may be passed in terms thereof.
1

## Page 294

4. The terms of the Settlement Agreement read as under:
“  5. Both the parties hereto have
arrived at an amicable settlement on
the following terms and conditions
for  dissolution  of  marriage  by
mutual consent:-
A. That the parties have agreed that
the Respondent-husband will pay to
the Petitioner-wife a total sum of
Rs. 12,00,000/- [Rupees Twelve Lakhs
Only]  towards  full  and  final
settlement of all her claims towards
her  permanent  alimony,  Stridhan,
maintenance (past, present, future),
and any other claim whatsoever.
B.  That  during  the  course  of
Mediation,  the  Petitioner-wife
presented a list of her jewellery
and articles on 01.05.2026 which is
annexed at Schedule A, which she had
brought with her to the matrimonial
home in Aurangabad, Maharashtra, and
demanded the return of the same. The
Respondent-husband, after reviewing,
confirmed  the  said  list  on
04.05.2026  which  is  annexed  at
Schedule  B,  and  accordingly,  the
Respondent-husband  has  agreed  to
return the said jewellery and Gift
articles to the Petitioner-wife on
28.06.2026  subject  to  it  being
ascertained and verified physically
2

## Page 295

by the Petitioner-wife or her family
member/representative.
C. It is agreed between the parties
that they will move an application
jointly before the Hon'ble Supreme
Court  under  Article  142  of  the
Constitution of India for invoking
inherent  powers  of  the  Hon'ble
Supreme Court, praying for divorce
by mutual consent, as the parties
have been staying separately since
May 2022, i.e., for the last more
than  4  years,  and  there  is  an
irretrievable  breakdown  of  the
marriage.
D. It is further agreed between the
parties that if the Hon'ble Supreme
Court  is  pleased  to  allow  the
application filed by both parties
under  Article  142  of  the
Constitution  of  India,  then  both
parties shall withdraw all the cases
filed  by  them,  if  any.  The
Respondent –husband will pay to the
Petitioner Wife a total sum of Rs.
12,00,000/-  [Rupees  Twelve  Lakhs
Only]  via  DD  in  the  name  of
Petitioner-wife  (Khushita  Manoj
Sharma) before the Hon'ble Court at
the time of hearing in the present
matter  on  the  Joint  Application
under Art. 142 of the Constitution
of India.
3

## Page 296

E. It is also agreed between the
parties  that  after  the  joint
application  under  Art.  142  of
Constitution of India is allowed,
neither  of  them  or  their  family
members  would  contact  or  try  to
contact with each other or their
family  members  directly  or
indirectly.
6.  That  the  Petitioner  and  the
Respondent have agreed that neither
of  them  will  initiate  any  other
legal action or complaint against
each other or against the family
members of each other in respect of
their  matrimonial  dispute  in  the
future.
7. That subject to the aforesaid
terms, the parties have resolved all
the disputes amicably in relation to
the marriage and have been left with
no  claims  against  each  other  or
their respective family members.
8. That by signing this Agreement,
the parties hereto solemnly state
and affirm that they have no further

other, including maintenance, or any
movable or immovable property, and
all  the  disputes  and  differences
have been amicably settled by the
4

## Page 297

parties hereto through the process
of mediation.
9. That the parties undertake to
abide by the terms and conditions
set  out  in  the  above  mentioned
Settlement  Agreement,  which  have
been arrived at with the free will
of the parties without any coercion,
duress  or  collusion  and  parties
undertake not to raise any dispute
whatsoever henceforth.
10. The contents of this settlement
agreement have been explained to all
the parties through their respective
counsels and they have understood
the same. ”
5. In terms of the settlement arrived at between the
parties, a Demand Draft dated 29.07.2026 bearing D.D.
No.014840, drawn in favour of the petitioner, for a sum
of  Rs.12,00,000/-,  has  been  handed  over  to  the
petitioner. A copy of the Demand Draft has been handed
over in the Court and is placed on record.
6. In view of the above, the following directions are
issued:
(i) The marriage solemnized on 27.01.2022 between the
petitioner and the respondent having broken down
irretrievably, is hereby dissolved by a decree of
divorce by mutual consent in exercise of the powers
5

## Page 298

conferred upon this Court under Article 142 of the
Constitution of India;
(ii) All  legal  proceedings,  as  mentioned  above,
pending  inter  se  the  parties  shall  stand
closed/quashed, as the case may be. The allegations
and counter-allegations made by the parties against
each other in the said proceedings, if any, shall be
deemed  to  have  been  withdrawn  and  shall  stand
expunged from the records;
(iii) Decree be drawn up accordingly. The Settlement
Agreement shall form part of the decree sheet;
(iv) It goes without saying that both parties shall
continue to abide by the terms and conditions of the
Settlement Agreement, without any exception;
(v) The Registry is directed to forward a copy of
this  order  to  the  Court/Authority  concerned  for
passing  appropriate  formal  orders  closing  the
proceedings/placing a copy of this order on the
record of the respective case file(s); and
(vi) The parties, through the learned counsel present
in the Court, have been apprised of the consequences
of any breach of the Settlement Agreement, including
initiation of appropriate proceedings for Contempt of
Court.
7. In view of the above facts and circumstances, I.A.
No.236265 of 2026 is allowed and the Transfer Petition
stands disposed of in terms of the aforesaid directions.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).             OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (C) No(s). 27485/2025)
MUNICIPAL COUNCIL, SRI GANGANAGAR      ...APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
CENTURY SALES                                                   …RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R 
1. Heard. Leave Granted.
2. This Appeal is directed against the order dated 09.01.2025
whereunder the Civil Miscellaneous Appeal No.1577 of 2024 came to
be dismissed and the judgment and decree dated 15.09.2023 passed in
Civil Suit No.99 of 2021 decreeing the suit and directing the
Appellant to refund a sum of Rs.92,00,000/- with interest thereon at
the rate of 9% per annum came to be affirmed. The Appellant
auctioned the advertisement rights for display of advertisements
within the jurisdiction of ULB at Sri Ganganagar for the year 2016-17
with a provision for extension upto two years. The Respondent herein
1

## Page 302

having participated in the auction and on being declared successful,
deposited 25% of the total bid amount of Rs.1,78,20,000/-. The
remaining 75% amount was to be deposited within 30 days and the
Respondent herein was required to sign a contract deed on stamp
paper. After repeated defaults on the part of respondent in not
depositing the balance amount of 75%, the Appellant was forced to
issue a notice, prior to which the Appellant blacklisted the Respondent
and  demanded  payment  of  outstanding  dues  and  damages.
Questioning the issuance of notice dated 14.10.2016, W.P. No.14323
of 2016 was filed by the Respondent herein which came to be
dismissed on 10.11.2017 by arriving at a conclusion that disputed
facts cannot be examined in a Writ Petition filed under Article 226 of
the Constitution of India. The further notice issued was also
challenged in W.P. No. 5881 of 2017 which did not yield any result.
The contract was cancelled and the Respondent was blacklisted on
28.08.2017. Again, the Respondent challenged the same in W.P.
No.1963 of 2018 which was dismissed as withdrawn by an order dated
05.09.2019.
2

## Page 303

3. In light of the dispute that had arisen between the parties, a Committee
was constituted by the appellant to look into the dispute and the said
Committee observed that the Municipal Council, had failed to
discharge its responsibilities under the contract which had caused
financial loss to the Respondent. On 03.03.2021, the Municipal
Council made a recommendation to the Director, Local Bodies to
refund the total amount deposited by the Respondent. On account of
no decision having been taken by the Department, Respondent filed a
suit in Civil Suit No.99 of 2021 for recovery which came to be
decreed for Rs.92,00,000/- with interest @ 9% per annum.
4. The aforesaid judgment and decree came to be challenged by the
appellant in the appeal did not yield any result.  In other words, it
came to be dismissed by upholding the judgment and decree of the
Trial Court. It was held by the Appellate Court, that Appellant had
breached the contractual obligations by failing to issue licenses and
allot sites on time, despite the Respondent having deposited
substantial amounts and being ready and willing to perform its part of
the contract. Infact, the counter claim raised by the Appellant before
3

## Page 304

the Trial Court which had been rejected had not been challenged by
the Appellant herein.
5. Having heard the learned Advocates appearing for the parties and on
perusal of the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court as
affirmed by the Appellate Court it would emerge from the records that
in the auction conducted for putting up the hoardings, the Respondent
was the successful bidder, namely the highest bidder and had to
deposit 25% of the total bid within the prescribed period which had
been deposited. However, the remaining 75% of the amount was not
fully deposited or in other words partial deposit was made. It has been
the case of the Respondent before the Courts below that despite
depositing the 25% amount plus certain other amounts, the contract
was not signed by the Appellant and for no fault of the Respondent,
the Appellant did not execute the contract, thereby caused financial
loss to the Respondent. On the other hand, it has been the consistent
stand of the Appellant that despite repeated notices issued to the
Respondent to deposit the balance 75% of the bid amount, same was
not paid or in other words, intermittent payments were made and as
such several notices were issued calling upon the Respondent to
4

## Page 305

deposit the balance amount with 18% interest. It is an undisputed fact
that respondent had challenged one such notice in Writ Petition
No.14323 of 2016 which came to be dismissed vide order dated
10.11.2017. Although it was the contention of the Appellant before
the courts below that, by virtue of the interim orders passed, the
Appellant was prevented from taking any coercive steps against the
Respondent and consequently the Respondent had continued to put up
the hoardings, the said contention was neither established nor
accepted. In other words, the counterclaim raised by the appellant in
that regard came to be rejected, and no appeal has been preferred
against such rejection.  In view of the fact that Committee constituted
by the Council itself had resolved to refund the amounts paid by the
Respondent and appellant having failed to make such payment, the
suit filed by the Respondent was rightly decreed upon appreciation of
the pleadings and evidence on record. The said judgment and decree
has been duly affirmed by the Appellate Court.
6. In view of the fact that Appellant was unable to recover the charges
for the alleged hoardings put up by the Respondent, we deem it
appropriate to put a quietus to this dispute by directing the Appellant
5

## Page 306

to pay a sum of Rs.1,00,00,000/- which is inclusive of interest as
against the judgment and decree passed for Rs.92,00,000/- with
interest @ 9% per annum as it would meet the ends of justice.
Accordingly, the Appeal is allowed in part, the judgment and decree
passed in Civil Suit No. 99 of 2021 dated 15.09.2023 as affirmed by
the High Court stands modified to the extent aforestated with no order
as to costs. Pending applications, if any, stand consigned to records.

petitioners.

Regulations are under active consideration.  It will be appreciated
if an appropriate decision with respect thereto is also taken
before the next date of hearing.

appointed as the Nodal Counsel for the petitioner(s) and Mr. Manoj
Ranjan Sinha (M.No.9811067271) is appointed as the Nodal Counsel
for  the  respondent(s).  Counsel  for  the  petitioner(s)/
intervenor(s)/impleader(s)  are  directed  to  supply  all  the
petitions/IAs to the Nodal Counsel(s), who may collate the issues
raised on their behalf. 
5. The counter affidavits may also be supplied to the Nodal
Counsel(s), who may collate the same for the purpose of further
consideration.  
6. Post  these  matters  for  further  consideration  on
05.11.2026.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. All the applications for impleadment/intervention are allowed, subject to
just exceptions at the time of final hearing.
2. Amended Memo of Parties, in each of the special leave petitions
(wherever required), be filed by the petitioners within two weeks from date.
3. Counter affidavits to the special leave petitions may be filed by all the
respondents within four weeks.
4. Rejoinder thereto, if any, may be filed by two weeks thereafter.
5. Re-list the special leave petitions in the week commencing 16th November,
2026.
6. Interim order, if any, shall continue till the next date of hearing.
7. It is reported that some of the respondents in all three special leave
petitions are common. If notice has already been issued to such of the common
respondents, further notice need not be served to them.

## Page 349

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Issue notice, returnable within six weeks.
3. The  petitioner before  this Court  has filed  the
present petition, being aggrieved by the impugned final
judgment dated 26.11.2024 passed by the High Court of
Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur in CRA No. 1612 of 2023, whereby
the  conviction  and  sentence  of  seven  years’  rigorous
imprisonment imposed upon the petitioner under Section 307
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, by the Special Judge,
Scheduled  Castes  and  Scheduled  Tribes  (Prevention  of
Atrocities) Act, Rajnandgaon, Chhattisgarh, in Special Case
No. 15 of 2021, was affirmed.
4. The petitioner has already undergone almost three
years and six months of the sentence out of the seven
years’ sentence awarded to him.
5. This Court, after hearing the learned counsel for
the petitioner and keeping in view the grounds raised on
behalf of the petitioner, is of the opinion that the prayer
for  suspension  of  sentence  deserves  to  be  allowed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.      /2026
(Arising out of SLP (C) No. 26505/2023
CENTURY CEMENT EDUCATION SOCIETY BAIKUNTH            Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
POSHAN LAL VERMA & ORS.
R-1: Poshan Lal Verma 
R-2: The District Education Officer, 
District Raipur, Chhattisgarh
R-3: State of Chhattisgarh, through 
The Secretary, Department of School
Education, D.K.S. Bhavan, Mantralay,
Raipur Chhattisgarh
                             Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Heard Dr. S. Muralidhar, learned Senior Counsel for the
petitioner,  Mr. Manohar Pratap, learned counsel for the respondent
No.1 and Ms. Ankita Sharma, learned AoR for the respondents No. 2
and 3.
2. Leave granted. 
3. The present appeal arises out of an order dated  07.09.2023
passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur in WA No.
352/2023 by which the appellants have been directed to reinstate
1

## Page 355

the respondent No.1 and pay full back wages to him. 
4. Learned Senior Counsel for the appellant submitted that the
High Court has not appreciated the basic issues with regard to
maintainability, as also the relevant law which would govern the
field in the facts and circumstances of the present case. Reliance
has been placed on the additional affidavit filed on behalf of
respondents No. 2 and 3, wherein a categorical stand has been taken
that the State has no role in either the recruitment of respondent
No. 1, as it was purely an unaided post, and in paragraph No. 6, a
categorical stand has been taken that with regard to teaching or
non-teaching staff appointed beyond the sanctioned grant-in-aid
post, they had to be paid from the private funds of the management,
i.e., the appellant-School, and further that the State does not
exercise control over them and the responsibility for such staff
rests solely with the management of the appellant-School. It was
pointed out that the State has clarified the matter that only in
respect of posts which are fully aided by the State Government, the
relevant Act/Rules/Regulations would be applicable.
5. Learned Senior Counsel further submitted that even with regard
to maintainability, this Court has consistently held that where
there was a purely private school managed by an independent and
non-State Managing Committee, the remedy would not lie by moving
under the writ jurisdiction of the High Court, but would be either
before  a  Statutory  Authority,  if  prescribed,  or,  in  the
alternative, under the common civil law, i.e., by filing a suit.
2

## Page 356

6. Learned counsel for the respondent No.1 submitted that the
relevant Act/Rules/Regulations would be applicable for the reason
that both the “institution”, “school” and “teacher” are defined and
irrespective of the mode of appointment as also whether it is an
aided or an un-aided school, there are certain safeguards to be
followed while terminating the service, dehors which the appellant
has acted in the present matter. Learned counsel has also addressed
the Court with regard to the case being maintainable before the
High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.
7. Having considered the matter in depth, we find that the issues
which have been raised before us on behalf of the appellant have
not been addressed. We further note that on the stand taken in the
additional affidavit of the respondents No. 2 and 3 (State and its
Authorities), the issue requires fresh consideration, especially
with regard to what has been indicated hereinabove. 
8. Accordingly, the matter is remanded to the High Court for
consideration afresh on all points and issues both on facts and in
law, as also that of maintainability of a Writ Petition under
Article 226 of the Constitution of India before the High Court in
the facts and circumstances of the present case.
9. Consequently, the appeal stands allowed, the impugned order
dated 07.09.2023 passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh at
Bilaspur in WA No. 352/2023 is set aside and Writ Appeal No.
352/2023 stands restored to its original file and number. The same
having already been finally decided, we request the High Court to
3

## Page 357

decide the same expeditiously. 
10. Parties would be at liberty to bring this order to the notice
of Hon’ble the Chief Justice of the High Court.
11. Before parting, we clarify that we have not expressed any
opinion on merits and all issues are left open for the High Court
to decide.
12. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

non-applicant and the respondent is the applicant.
2. The subject matter is the debt due from the non-
applicant to the applicant. Before the High Court, the
issue was with respect to dishonor of a cheque issued by

## Page 373

2
the non-applicant. Suffice it to notice that the non-
applicant has a history of flouting its own undertaking
so blatantly that we cannot but say that their conduct so
far is  reprehensible. However,  in resolution  of the
dispute, we have been attempting to effect the sale of
properties owned by the non-applicant, so as to fully
satisfy the debt due to the applicant, as agreed upon by
both the parties in our order dated 26.03.2025.
3. The order relevant being of 24.03.2026, is extracted
hereinunder:-
“1.  The  above  Miscellaneous  Applications  have
been filed by the petitioner and the respondent
in the Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.2018 of
2024 disposed of by order dated 26.03.2025. We
shall refer to the parties from the status in the
SLP. After a spate of settlements which did not
fructify due to the default of the petitioner,
the respondent, to enable the satisfaction of the
debt due to it, agreed to yet another settlement
before this Court resulting in the order dated
26.03.2025. 
2. By the said order, this Court directed the
subject  property  to  be  placed  under  the
receivership of Principal District Judge, Mysuru,
Karnataka  (referred  to  herein  after  as  the
Receiver). The petitioner was given liberty to
negotiate and arrange for sale of property as one
whole or in parts within a period of nine months
from the date of disposal of the case. Out of the
total proceeds obtained, Rs.10,25,00,000/- along
with simple interest at the rate of 11% per annum
from 11.01.2023 was to be paid to the respondent.
To facilitate such payment the proceeds of the
sale were directed to be deposited before the
Receiver who was directed to disburse the amounts
to the respondent. The other directions are not
relevant  for  disposal  of  the  Miscellaneous
Applications filed.  
3. The application filed by the petitioner seeks
discharge of the Receiver since it is stated that

## Page 374

3
there is a bottle neck in facilitating a sale
since the Banks, obliged to follow Reserve Bank
of  India  guidelines,  on  loans  sanctioned  for
purchase of landed properties issue Demand Drafts
(DD)  only  at  the  time  of  execution  and
registration of sale deeds, which DDs are then
handed over to the seller. The Receiver insists
for the DD drawn on the Principal District Judge
to be handed over at the time when an endorsement
is made as the Receiver of the property in the
sale  deed  for  execution  and  presentation  for
registration.  This  results  in  the  Banks
expressing reluctance to finance a purchase for
reason of the prior issuance of DD being in
violation of the RBI guidelines. 
4. The respondent on the other hand by their
Miscellaneous  Application  proposes  that  the
balance  properties,  remaining  after  the  sales
already effected, shall be purchased by them at
the highest price for which small parcels of the
property  were  sold  from  the  larger  extent.
However, the price shown in the present sale
agreements, referred to in the I.A., are said to
be in tune with the market value. It is the
respondent’s contention that the petitioner has
not complied with the order passed and the debt
substantially  remains  outstanding.  The
application to relieve the Receiver itself is a
tactic to delay repayment and somehow get the
property out of the custody of the Receiver. The
respondent also offers a higher price, as this
Court may deem fit.  
5. We cannot fault the Principal District Judge
in insisting for the payment before making an
endorsement, especially since she is appointed as
a  Receiver  of  the  properties  on  our  orders.
However, considering the difficulty pointed out
by  the  petitioner  and  also  reckoning  the
apprehension of the respondent that sale may be
effected for a higher price which would not be
reflected in the sale deed, jeopardizing their
claim/charge on the property without ensuring the
full satisfaction of their debt as per the orders
of this Court, we make the following orders: 
i) The petitioner shall be entitled to negotiate
and facilitate the sale of the subject property
or its parcels as directed in the order dated
26.03.2025 by presenting the agreement of sale,
with the consideration shown therein before the
Receiver with a copy to the respondent.   

## Page 375

4
ii) If the consideration is not less than the
market value, then a draft sale deed shall be
presented, on the same consideration shown in the
agreement along with a communication regulating
sanction of loan from the bank financing the
purchase of plot, based on which the Receiver
shall make endorsement for carrying out the sale
and registration, clearly indicating that the DD
shall  be  issued  in  the  name  of  the
Receiver/Principal District Judge. 
iii) On the endorsement made by the Principal
District  Judge  in  the  draft  sale  deed  the
financing bank shall issue the DD as stipulated
in the endorsement, based on which the sale deed
shall be executed and registered. 
iv) The DD shall be handed over to the Receiver
who shall negotiate it as directed in our order.
v)  It  is  the  petitioner’s  obligation  to
facilitate the sale as per the sale agreement on
the consideration specified therein and if not
facilitated it shall be treated as a violation of
the terms of the agreement, the consequences of
which the petitioner will invite. 
vi) If the consideration is less than the market
value, at the discretion of the Receivers, the
respondent will be entitled to exercise the first
refusal,  indicating  that  if  the  respondent
desires he shall agree to purchase the property
on the consideration shown therein and the same
shall be set off against the amounts due to the
respondent  based  on  which  the  Receiver  shall
issue the endorsement on the sale deed to be
executed in favour of the respondent, which shall
be registered. 
6. The above exercise shall be completed within a
period of five months, failing which appropriate
orders will be passed in M.A.No.74 of 2026 filed
by the respondent. If the amounts due to the
respondent as per our order is satisfied, then
necessarily further directions in our order dated
26.03.2025 shall be given effect to. 
7. M.A. Diary No.7339 of 2026 is disposed of and
M.A.  No.74  of  2026  is  to  be  listed  on
14.07.2026.”
4. The matter was posted before us, specifically on the
plea raised by the applicant that the properties sold in
small parcels, are being sold for less than the market

## Page 376

5
value. We see that the objections were raised by the
applicant before the Principal District Judge ( in short
‘PDJ’),  Mysuru,  Karnataka,  who  is  appointed  as  the
Receiver,  but  later  they  consented  to  the  sale
transaction. 
5. As of now, it is submitted that the applicant has
received Rs.1,92,70,000/- and about Rs.4,59,60,000/- is
remaining with the PDJ, which is in the process of being
disbursed.
6. Considering the prayer made by the applicant, we had
stayed further sales on 14.07.2026, especially since none
was appearing for the non-applicant.
7. Considering the contentions raised by the applicant,
we  are  of  the  opinion  that  before  further  sale  is
conducted, we should get the details of the sales already
carried out. We, hence, direct the PDJ, the Receiver
appointed by us by order dated 26.03.2025, to furnish us
a chart showing the division of the total properties, the
parcels sold, the market price, the actual sale price
obtained  with  the  details  also  of  the  properties
remaining to be sold, with their market value.
8. We direct that in those matters where the sale was
proceeded with and the demand drafts are already in the
possession  of  the  PDJ,  the  PDJ  shall  take  further
proceedings to facilitate the sale of such properties,

## Page 377

6
the details of which shall also be included in the chart
furnished to us.
9. Insofar as the further requests for sale, the same
shall be kept in abeyance till a report is submitted to
us.
10. We also require the PDJ to give us a Statement of
Account of the amounts already disbursed to the applicant
and that remaining with the PDJ.
11. The applicant shall also give a computation of the
amounts  due,  the  credits  received  and  the  interest
applied, as indicated in our order dated 26.03.2025, so
as to get a clear picture of what is the balance due. The
Statement of Accounts shall indicate the balance due as
on 30.09.2026 and 31.10.2026.
12. The Registry shall communicate a copy of this order
to the PDJ, Mysuru, Karnataka. The applicant and the non-
applicant shall also produce a copy of this order before
the PDJ, Mysuru, Karnataka.
13. The matter shall be posted on 15.09.2026.

STATE OF RAJASTHAN & ORS.             RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Heard learned counsel appearing for the parties.
2. Leave granted.
3. The Special Leave Petition arises from the order
dated  29.06.2026  in  D.B.  Special  Appeal  Writ  No.
423/2026.
4. The appeal is pending before the Division Bench of
the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan, Bench at
Jaipur.
5. The appeal is admitted and, as an interim measure,
the order impugned has been passed by the Division Bench.
The learned counsel appearing for the appellant contends
that granting an interim stay is one of the procedures
followed by Division Bench with a view to preventing the
successful party from executing the order under challenge
in the appeal but issuing a direction though coached in a
liberal expression virtually amounts to allowing the writ

## Page 384

2
appeal  and  circumstanes  would  become  Fait  Accompli .
Therefore, while not objecting to granting the interim
stay  of  the  learned  Single  Judge’s  Judgment  dated
12.03.2026, emphasis is laid to the last sentence in the
order impugned.
6. Mr. Rahul Kaushik, learned senior counsel for the
appellant contends that this sentence is read out of
context,  and  the  consideration  of  totality  of
circumstances  would  convince  this  Court  that  the
direction has been issued in the larger interest of the
villagers, including his client who has a valid mining
lease in his favour.
7. We have taken note of the submissions and perused
the record.
8. Having perused the order dated 12.03.2026 of the
learned Single Judge, we are of the view that the last
sentence in the order impugned is rendering the pending
writ appeal Fait  Accompli. Therefore, the last sentence
in the impugned order to wit “The appellant would be free
to  construct  the  culvert  over  the  water  body  and  take
care that the flow of the water body remains continuous”,
needs interference and is set aside.
9. The parties are given liberty to request the High
Court for early hearing and we have no doubt that the
High Court would do the needful.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 926 OF 2016
AKHILESH KUMAR & ORS. ...Appellants
VERSUS
STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH           ...Respondent
WITH
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 981 OF 2016
O R D E R
1) The appellants have been charged for the offences
punishable under Sections 498-A, 306, 201 read with Section
34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘the IPC’) in
connection with F.I.R. No. 126 of 2005 registered at Police
Station – Dohru, District – Bilaspur, Himachal Pradesh and
were acquitted by the Trial Court  vide  its order dated
29.09.2010 in Sessions Trial No. 2/7 of 2006.  The High
Court of Himachal Pradesh  vide the impugned order dated
29.07.2016  set  aside  the  order  of  the  Trial  Court,
convicted the appellants, and sentenced them to undergo
rigorous imprisonment for a period of 10 years. Aggrieved,
the appellants are before us.
2) The case of the prosecution, in a nutshell, is that
on 16.10.2005 at 4.30 am, the deceased who was the wife of
the appellant/accused No.1 committed suicide by consuming
1

## Page 399

poison.  Admittedly,  at  that  point  of  time,  the
appellant/accused No.1 was not at home.
3) The Trial Court rendered an acquittal  inter  alia
holding that the evidence of PW-1 and PW-2, who are the
parents of the deceased, cannot be accepted.  Apart from
the fact that they are not the eyewitnesses, there are
material contradictions in the statements, particularly,
the allegation that the appellants have committed the
offences punishable under Section 302 of the IPC.  The Trial
Court incidentally was pleased to hold that the allegations
also do not make out the charge under Section 498-A of the
IPC, in view of the fact that they are very vague as they
did not point out the specific instances.  No independent
witnesses have been examined and the alleged suicide note
is inconclusive insofar as the signature of the deceased is
concerned.  The case of the prosecution that the suicide
note was written by one of the appellants/accused, was also
found to be not proved in view of the Report of the State
Forensic Science Laboratory. 
4) The High Court while acknowledging the fact that
there are omissions in the investigation done by the
prosecution, drew adverse inference against the appellants.
It heavily relied upon the evidence of PW-1 and PW-2
without much discussion on the suicide note and thus, did
2

## Page 400

not go into the allegations qua the other appellants.  The
fact that the appellant/accused No.1 was not even present
at  the  time  of  incident,  was  not  given  due  care.
Furthermore,  the  High  Court  did  not  find  anything
specifically wrong with the reasoning recorded by the Trial
Court.
5) We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties. 
6) When an order of acquittal is rendered by a Court of
first instance, the best presumption in favour of the
accused becomes strengthened.  It would, thus, become a
case of double presumption.  On a perusal of the impugned
judgment, we find that the High Court did not even take care
to consider the relevant material including the findings
rendered by the Trial Court, which had the benefit of
hearing  the  statements  of  the  witnesses  in  person.
Furthermore, the charge under Section 306 of the IPC would
stand proved based upon the foundational facts.  Along with
the foundational facts, it should also be proved that the
appellants/accused are desirous of instigating the deceased
to commit suicide. Certainly, these materials are not
available in the case at hand. The High Court merely went
on a moral ground and overturned the well merited judgment
of the Trial Court without even assailing the findings
3

## Page 401

recorded thereunder.
7) In such view of the matter, we are inclined to set
aside the impugned order passed by the High Court, and
acquit the appellants of all the charges, by restoring the
order passed by the Trial Court.
8) Accordingly, the impugned order passed by the High
Court stands set aside and the order dated 29.09.2010
passed by the Trial Court in Sessions Trial No. 2/7 of
2006, stands restored.  Bail bonds in favour of the
appellants shall stand discharged.
9) Insofar  as  the  termination  of  service  of  the
appellant/accused No.1 is concerned, we do not wish to
record anything as it is for the appellant No.1 to seek
appropriate remedy in the manner known to law.
10) Accordingly, the appeals stand disposed of in the
above terms.
11) Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.
………………………………………………………J.
                          (M.M. SUNDRESH)
………………………………………………………J.
                     (PRASANNA B. VARALE)
NEW DELHI;
AUGUST 19, 2026.

1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by Order dated 31.03.2026, passed by
the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (briefly the ‘High Court’
hereinafter) rejecting the bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant is the husband of the deceased wife. He has been
made an accused in Case Crime No.275/2024, registered at Police
Station – Moth in the District of Jhansi, Uttar Pradesh, under
Sections 85 and 80(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for
short, ‘BNS’) read with Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition
Act, 1961.
5. Case of the prosecution is that appellant and the other family
members had tortured the victim for dowry and unable to bear such
torture and humiliation, she allegedly hanged herself.
1

## Page 414

6. Appellant is in jail since 18.11.2024.
7. This Court by Order dated 08.06.2026 had issued notice,
pursuant to which respondent-State has filed counter affidavit.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant drew our attention to the
contents of the First Information Report as per which it is alleged
that deceased was subjected to physical abuse. However, he submits
that the medical evidence including the testimony of the Doctor PW-
5 (Page Nos. 93 to 95 of the paper book) says that no injury marks
due to beatings were found on the body of the deceased. Death due
to hanging by noose is possible. On the body of the deceased, no
mark of any operation before her death was found. He also submits
that there is material contradiction in the deposition of the
informant from what he had stated in the First Information Report.
In such circumstances, appellant deserves to be enlarged on bail.
9. Mr. Banerjee, learned State Counsel, however, submits that
statutory presumption is against the appellant. The deceased had
died an unnatural death in the matrimonial home within 7 years of
marriage. At this stage, it would be premature to come to any
conclusion about the culpability or otherwise of the appellant.
Trial is ongoing satisfactorily. Out of 19 witnesses cited, 6 have
been examined. Therefore, appellant may not be enlarged on bail at
this stage.
10. We  have  given  our  anxious  consideration  to  the  rival
submissions made at the Bar. We have also considered the materials
on record.
11. Without expressing any opinion on merit, we are of the view
that having regard to the period of incarceration undergone by the
2

## Page 415

appellant and the possibility of the trial being concluded in the
near future being remote, we are inclined to enlarge the appellant
on bail.
12. Accordingly, we set aside the order of the High Court dated
31.03.2026 and direct that the appellant shall be produced before
the Jurisdictional Sessions Court within a maximum period of 7 days
from today whereafter he shall be enlarged on bail on such terms
and conditions as may be deemed appropriate
13. Appeal is accordingly allowed.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Heard learned counsel for the appellant-victim/complainant,

granting anticipatory bail to the respondent No.2 herein and
27.10.2025, passed by the High Court of Calcutta, Circuit Bench at
Jalpaiguri, in CRM(A) No. 770/2025, by which the prayer of the
appellant-victim/complainant for modification of the order dated
16.10.2025 passed by the High Court was rejected.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant-victim/complainant submits
that the appellant-victim/complainant had a right to oppose the
prayer for grant of anticipatory bail to respondent No. 2, but an
order was passed on 16.10.2025 granting anticipatory bail to the
1

## Page 419

respondent No.2 behind his back. Learned counsel submitted that the
order itself would show that the appellant-victim/complainant was
not heard, as the date fixed in the case was subsequently changed
but the change of date was not intimated to him. Learned counsel
submitted that the order impugned dated 27.10.2025 also records the
fact that the learned counsel for the respondent No. 2 had not
intimated the said change of date to the learned counsel for the
appellant-victim/complainant  herein.  Learned  counsel  contended
that, on merits also, the grant of anticipatory bail without any
discussion on merits was unwarranted and unjustified in the facts
and circumstances of the present case.
5. Learned counsel for the respondent No.1-State of West Bengal
submits  that  the  plea  of  the  appellant-victim/complainant  is
correct. She has further submitted that subsequent to the grant of
anticipatory bail to the respondent No.2, he had entered into the
jurisdiction of the Police Station of the complainant and had
threatened the appellant-victim/complainant.
6. Learned counsel for respondent No. 2 submitted that it was the
duty of the learned counsel for the appellant-victim/complainant to
be vigilant and to remain informed about the date of hearing, and
that his choosing not to appear would not be a ground for
interference with the order passed by the High Court. However, he
could not dispute the fact that the Court had not even noticed the
absence  of  the  learned  counsel  for  the
appellant-victim/complainant.
7. Having considered the matter, we find that the matter needs
reconsideration on merits. Accordingly, the impugned order stands
2

## Page 420

set aside. The case is restored to its original file and number
before the High Court. The same would be heard afresh on merits
after  hearing  learned  counsel  for  the  parties  including  the
appellant-victim/complainant.
8. We have been informed that pursuant to the order impugned, the
respondent No.2 has appeared before the Court below and has been
released on bail. In such view of the matter, we find it equitable
that the respondent No.2 remains on bail till the High Court takes
a fresh view in the matter.
9. Thus, we request the High Court to consider the matter and
pass orders expeditiously and preferably within six weeks from
today. The parties shall bring the present order to the notice of

fresh consideration.

O R D E R
    1.  Leave granted.
2.  The present appeal has been filed by the appellants
being aggrieved by the impugned order passed by the
High  Court  of  Judicature  at  Patna  in  Criminal
Miscellaneous No.28956 of 2026, rejecting the bail
petition of the appellants.
3. Learned counsel for the appellants has argued
before this Court that the consignor and consignee of
the codeine cough syrup both have been granted bail and
the appellants are the driver and cleaner with no
criminal antecedents.
4.  On the other hand, learned counsel appearing on
behalf of the respondent-State of Bihar has vehemently
opposed the prayer for grant of bail. However, after
hearing the learned counsel for the parties and going
through the material available on records, this Court
is of the view that their further detention is not
necessary pending trial and, therefore, we allow the
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRIMINAL) NO.  11786/2026  ]

## Page 444

2
appeal and grant relief as prayed for by admitting the
appellants to an order of grant of bail. 
5. Appellants shall be released on bail, subject to
furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the
trial  court  and  subject  to  such  other  terms  and
conditions as may be imposed by it. 
6. Needless to observe, the appellants shall not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat or
promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the facts
of the case from disclosing such facts to the court.
7. In the event there is any breach of the terms and
conditions for grant of bail, the trial court shall be
at liberty to cancel the bail of the appellants.
8.  It  is  also  ordered  that  the  appellants  shall
diligently attend proceedings of the trial, unless
exempted. If he is found to abstain from attending the
proceedings without justifiable cause, that could also
be seen as breach of the conditions for grant of bail
and the trial court will be free to pass appropriate
orders.
9. We clarify that the observations made in this order
and grant of bail will not be treated as findings on
the merits of the case.
10.  The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed  on  the
aforesaid  terms,  and  the  impugned  order  dated
01.05.2026 is set aside.
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRIMINAL) NO.  11786/2026  ]

that from the allegations itself it appears that
1

the relationship between the appellant and the

evidence and in the trial, victim’s mother (PW1)

any opinion on merits of the prosecution case, we

order passed by the High Court rejecting the bail
prayer of the appellant is set aside.

of the case.

2. In this case, when the matter came up on 02.02.2026 for

## Page 459

2
1. Delay condoned.
2.  Heard  Mr.  R.Subramanian,  learned  senior  counsel
appearing for the petitioner. The learned senior counsel
contends that the judgment of the Constitution Bench in
the case titled as “Central Organisation for Railway
Elecrification vs. M/s. ECI Spci Smo Mcml (JV) A Joint
Venture Company”, reported in (2025) 4 SCC 641 (4(2) for
short) though prospective, is only prospective for three
members tribunals. Particular attention is drawn to para
169 (at SCC page 755). Learned senior counsel also
relies  on  the  judgment  of  this  Court  in  “Bhadra
International  (India)Pvt.Ltd.&  Ors.  vs.  Airport
Authority of India” reported in 2026 SCC OnLine page 7,
particularly  para  120,  to  contend  that  since  the
constitution of the tribunal was without jurisdiction,
the award is unenforceable.
3. Issue notice, returnable on 20th April, 2026.
4. In the meantime, there shall be stay of execution
proceedings in EPR No.18/2024 pending on the file of III
Additional District Court at Gobichettipalayam, Erode
District, Tamil Nadu.”
3. The issue arises out of a transport contract agreement
between the petitioner and respondent- HPCL, Mangalore,
dated 25.07.2012. Thereafter, disputes arose between the
parties.  The  respondent-  HPCL  invoked  the  arbitration
clause under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
According to the learned counsel for the petitioner, the
respondent- HPCL appoint a sole arbitrator unilaterally and
the arbitrator was one of the officials of the respondent-
HPCL. The HPCL filed a claim of Rs.23,83,033.67. Thereafter
on 01.06.2017 an ex-parte award for Rs.13,13,606.03 came to

## Page 460

3
be passed. The petitioner who had initially participated,
thereafter  stopped  from  participating  before  the
arbitrator. The present matter arises out of an execution
proceedings.
4. Today, we are not required to elaborately consider the
issues, since respondent- HPCL has unequivocally stated
before  us  that  without  going  into  the  merits  of  the
contentions of the parties arising herein, the award dated
01.06.2017 against the petitioner, can be set aside.
5. Parties have consented before us that the matter can
be  referred  to  arbitration  of  the  Arbitration  Centre
attached to the  High Court of Judicature at Madras for
appointment of sole arbitrator, who shall adjudicate the
dispute between the parties afresh.
6. In view of the consent recorded herein, the award
dated 01.06.2017 and all consequential proceedings arising
there on, are set aside.
7. The matter is referred to the Arbitration Centre
attached to the High Court of Judicature at Madras for
necessary action at their end. 
8. Parties to appear on 31.08.2026 at 2.00 PM before the

1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by Order dated 04.08.2025, passed by
High Court of Chhatisgarh (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter)
rejecting the bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant has been named as an accused in Crime No.359/2025,
registered at Police Station Sarkanda, District Bilaspur in the
State of Chhatisgarh, under Section 20(B) of the Narcotic Drugs and
Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for short, ‘NDPS Act’).
5. Allegation against the appellant is that on 06.03.2025 at
about 17:00 hours, based on secret information, police intercepted
a motor cycle and from the possession of the rider of the motor
cycle Vikas Verma, 7.9 kgs of Ganja were recovered and additional 3
kgs of ganja were recovered from under the seat cover of the motor
1

## Page 515

cycle. Thus, total ganja seized was 10.9 kgs. The pillion rider-
Sameer Verma, escaped from the scene. Appellant has been named in
the disclosure statement of accused Vikas Verma who stated that the
contraband was meant for the appellant.
6. Appellant was arrested on 14.05.2025 and since then he has
been in custody.
7. This Court  vide  order dated 20.07.2026 had issued notice
whereafter State has filed counter affidavit.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that no contraband
was recovered from the appellant. Appellant came to be implicated
only on the disclosure statement of the accused-Vikas Verma.
Contraband seized is below the commercial quantity. Both accused
Vikas Verma and Sameer Verma have been enlarged on bail. Therefore,
the appellant may be released on bail.
9. Learned State Counsel referring to the averments made in the
counter affidavit submits that trial is in progress. Though 19
witnesses  have  been  cited,  1  witness  has  been  examined  and
discharged. If the Court directs, the trial can be expedited. That
apart, he submits that appellant has an antecedent of committing
similar offence. High Court has taken note of this fact while
declining bail. Therefore, at this stage, appellant may not be
enlarged on bail.
10. Responding to the aforesaid submission, learned counsel for
the appellant submits that in so far the antecedent is concerned,
that too pertains to contraband much below the commercial quantity.
Appellant has been granted bail in the said case.
11. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties have
2

## Page 516

received the due consideration of the Court.
12. Appellant is in custody for more than 1 year 3 months now.
There is no possibility of the trial concluding in the near future.
Considering the above and the fact that the contraband seized was
from the co-accused and not from that of the appellant and is below
the commercial quantity, we are inclined to grant bail to the
appellant.
13. Accordingly, we set aside the order of the High Court dated
04.08.2025 and direct that the appellant shall be produced before
the Special Court within a maximum period of 7 days from today
whereafter  he  shall  be  released  on  bail  on  such  terms  and
conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
14. Since learned State counsel made a statement that appellant is
from the State of Odisha, we direct that the appellant shall appear
on each and every date of the ongoing trial without fail except on
occasions when it is beyond his control.
15. Appeal is accordingly allowed.
16. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant has been named as an accused in Case Crime No.16 of
2025, registered at Police Station Sikhera, District Muzzafarnagar
in the State of Uttar Pradesh, under Sections 5J(ii)/6 of the
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012.
4. Allegation against the appellant is that appellant had entered
into physical relation with the victim, who was a minor, because of
which she became pregnant.
5. Appellant was arrested and is in custody since 08.02.2025.
6. By the impugned order dated 24.11.2025, High Court rejected
the bail application of the appellant.
7. This Court by Order dated 14.07.2026, had issued notice,
pursuant to which respondent-State has filed counter affidavit.
1

## Page 519

8. Learned counsel for the appellant has drawn the attention of
the Court to the statement made by the so-called victim and submits
that she had herself stated in her deposition that she was about 17
years of age and that she had an affair with the appellant. They
had gone together to Patna on 29.01.2025, where they stayed
together as husband and wife. He would, therefore, submit that it
is a consensual relationship. It is an incidental fact that the so-
called victim turned out to be below 18 years of age.
9. On the other hand, learned State counsel submits that going by
the school certificate, the victim was around 16 years of age when
appellant established physical relationship with her. She was also
found to be pregnant. Trial in this case is proceeding smoothly.
Out of the 11 cited witnesses, 3 have been examined. In fact, on
the last occasion, it was the appellant’s side which did not turn
up  to  cross-examine  the  witness.  Therefore,  at  this  stage,
appellant may not be enlarged on bail.
10. On a query by the Court, as to whether the so-called victim
has delivered the child since she was stated to be 8 weeks pregnant
at the time of lodging of the First Information Report, learned
State counsel submits that he has no instructions in this regard as
of today.
11. To this statement, learned counsel for the appellant submits
that the so called victim has not delivered any child. Only to
cover up the so-called family honor, the First Information Report
was lodged against the appellant whereafter he has been kept in
detention since 08.02.2025.
12. Having regard to the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the
2

## Page 520

case and the fact that appellant is in custody for more than one
and a half years now, we are of the view that appellant should be
enlarged on bail.
13. We, accordingly, set aside the impugned order of the High
Court dated 24.11.2025 and direct that the appellant shall be
produced before the Trial Court within a maximum period of 7 days
from today whereafter he shall be enlarged on bail on such terms
and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
14. It goes without saying that both parties shall cooperate with
the ongoing trial.
15. Appeal is accordingly allowed.
16. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The land in question, admeasuring 7 Kanals and 18 Marlas
in Survey No. 525, Mouza Kangan, District Gandebal, was
utilized by the State for construction of a Police Station,
way back in the year 1953. The State allegedly did not
follow  or  comply  with  the  acquisition  procedure  for
diverting  the  said  land  for  such  public  purpose.  The
appellant is stated to be one of the co-owners of the land.
3. It seems that the appellant slept over his rights
regarding the said land for 68 years, whereafter he finally
made representations to various authorities only in 2020.
Subsequently, he moved a writ petition before the High
Court, questioning the forcible acquisition/utilisation of
his land. The High Court has dismissed the writ petition by
way of the impugned order, primarily on the ground of
inordinate  delay  in  filing  the  writ  petition  and
consequential acquiescence on the part of the appellant.
1

## Page 531

4. In our considered opinion, the reasoning assigned by the
High Court for dismissing the petition of the appellant
cannot be accepted, especially in light of two decisions of
this Court in  Tukaram Kana Joshi & Ors.  vs.  Maharashtra
Industrial Development Corporation & Ors. , (2013) 1 SCC 353
and Vidya Devi vs. State of Himachal Pradesh & Ors., (2020)
2 SCC 569. It bears reiteration that once it is admitted by
the State that the land was utilised for a public purpose,
in this case, the construction of a police station, without
acquiring the same, it is imperative that the due amount of
compensation be paid to the respective landowner(s). The
respondents need to be sensitive towards the Constitutional
rights of landowners, and private property cannot be taken
over without following the prescribed procedure in law. The
Appellant herein is, thus, entitled to his share in the fair
compensation due for the divestment of the land.  
5. That being said, while determining the said amount of
compensation payable to the appellant, the inordinate delay
on  his  part  in  agitating  his  claims  can  also  not  be
overlooked.
6. Taking  into  consideration  all  the  attending
circumstances, it seems to us that the ends of justice would
be  adequately  met  by  awarding  the  compensation  to  the
appellant as would have been admissible in the year 1953.
However, in view of the delay on account of the appellant,
statutory interest shall only be admissible from the date on
which the writ petition was filed before the High Court. The
2

## Page 532

Appellant shall also be entitled to compensation for rental
occupation of the land, without interest, from 1953 till
date.
7. Hence, the appeal is partly allowed, and the impugned
order passed by the High Court is set aside. For the purpose
of assessing the amount payable to the appellant, the matter
is  remitted  to  the  High  Court.  The  competent  Land
Acquisition Collector may pass an appropriate Award-cum-
Order within three months, and the same shall be placed
before  the  High  Court  for  its  consideration  and  final
orders.
......................CJI.
(SURYA KANT)
........................J.  
(JOYMALYA BAGCHI) 
........................J.  
(V. MOHANA) 
       
NEW DELHI;        
AUGUST 17, 2026

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.      /2026
(Arising out of SLP(C)No. 7546/2022)
A. JENIX DEV SINGH                                 Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
R BALACHANDRAN                                     Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Heard Mr. Shoeb Alam, learned Senior Counsel for the appellant
and  Mr.  M.  Sathyanarayan,  learned  Senior  Counsel  for  the
respondent.
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal arises out of an order dated 23.07.2020
passed by the Madras High Court in CRPNPD No. 2747/2018, by which
the Revision filed by the respondent was allowed, and the matter
was remanded for fresh consideration by the Execution Court.
4. The appellant succeeded in the suit filed by him for specific
performance against the brother of the respondent. The same was
upheld up to this Court. When the appellant moved for execution of
the decree in his favour, the respondent appeared and objected,
stating that being the brother, he had  a share in the property in
dispute and was never heard at any stage and thus should be allowed
to contest. The Execution Court rejected the same on the ground
that he was  a partner in the partnership firm, which  was the
1

## Page 535

original owner of the suit property. However, in revision, by the
impugned order, the said order has been reversed.
5. Learned Senior Counsel for the appellant submitted that this
is  a  clear  case  of  how  the  process  of  the  Court  has  been
abused/misused. It was submitted that the suit was filed in the
year 2008 and attained finality on 09.04.2018, when this Court, by
order dated 09.04.2018 passed in SLP (C) No. 10609 of 2018,
dismissed the Special Leave Petition. It was submitted that when
the appellant moved for execution to get the fruits of his victory
before the Court, the matter was sought to be relegated for a de
novo trial, which this Court would take serious note of.
6. Learned Senior Counsel for the respondent submitted that the
respondent was a partner in the partnership firm which was the
owner of the suit property and that, even if there was delay in
raising such plea, before final delivery of possession in execution
proceedings, he had a right to be heard and agitate the same. It
was submitted that ultimately, the fact would remain that a partner
of a firm, which is the owner of the suit property, is deprived of
his right of being duly represented and of contesting a case of
specific performance when a property of the firm is sought to be
alienated.
7. Having considered the matter, we find that the issue is
absolutely a bogey created by the respondent to defeat a genuine
and  bona fide claim which had been upheld by three Courts,
including this Court. We are not inclined to give the benefit of
doubt to the respondent on the ground that he was unaware of the
2

## Page 536

proceedings which were being contested by his brother, who was
undoubtedly a member of the partnership firm. Further, as has been
indicated to us by learned Senior Counsel for the appellant, the
counsel who had represented the brother of the respondent before
the Court below in the earlier litigation was the same counsel who
had filed the present objection on behalf of the respondent.
8. Be that as it may, we find that the objection itself was
frivolous and  that the Execution Court had rightly rejected the
same. In such circumstances, the interference by the High Court was
improper.
9. Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed. The impugned order
dated 23.07.2020 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras
in CRPNPD No. 2747/2018 is set aside. The order dated 17.07.2018 in
E.A SR No. No. 1300 of 2018 in E.P No. 206 of 2017 in 0.S No. 144
of 2008 of the Executing Court stands restored.  Consequences to
follow.
10. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

.....................J.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The  Central  Bureau  of  Investigation  (CBI)  has  filed  a
compliance  affidavit  pursuant  to  the  order  dated  28.07.2026,
explaining  the  coordination  meetings  held  between  various
investigating agencies, SFIO, and RBI. It is explained that the
first five sets of allegations in the complaint by the Directorate
of Enforcement have already been investigated by the Economic
Offences Wing, Delhi Police. It is further submitted that a
parallel investigation may not be advisable. With regard to the
sixth allegation, re:  quid-pro-quo  involving a sum of Rs. 1574
crores, it is stated that the CBI has sought permission from the
Special Court for further investigation, and an application to this
effect has also been moved before the Special Judge (PMLA), Mumbai,
statedly listed for hearing on 24.08.2026. We direct the Special
Judge to decide that application in accordance with law and pass
appropriate orders within two weeks from 24.08.2026. The CBI shall,
thereafter, submit a fresh status report.
3

## Page 557

2. The CBI is further directed to inquire into the aforementioned
five allegations, regardless of the opinion/report of EOW, Delhi
Police. A comprehensive report, accordingly, shall be filed by the
CBI.
3. Meanwhile, the status report of the EOW, Delhi Police, which
is on record, has also been considered. While we do not express any
opinion with respect to the part of the report, which gives a clean
chit to certain transactions, especially in light of the separate
direction to the CBI, we further direct the EOW, Delhi Police to
complete its pending investigation with respect to the sixth
transaction and file a fresh status report.
4. Post these matters for further consideration on 29.09.2026.

        UPON hearing the counsel the Court made 
the following
                      O R D E R
1. The petitioner who had been denied regular
bail by the High Court, has been in judicial
custody since 13.06.2022, which is a period of
more than 4 years and 2 months, in connection with
FIR No.104/2022 filed at PS Adityapur, District
Seraikela, Jharkhand for the offence punishable
under Sections 302, 201, 120B, and 34 of the
Indian  Penal  Code  (for  short  “the  IPC”)  and
Sections 25(1-B)(a), 26, and 27 of the Arms Act,
1959 (for short “the Arms Act”).
2. The Chargesheet had been filed on 05.09.2022,
and the charges were framed on 07.12.2022.
3. The allegation relates to an incident of a
fight between two groups, with the petitioner and
two of the co-accused on one side, and the three
SLP (Crl.) No.14592/2026 2

## Page 560

deceased victims on the other. The fight was
allegedly motivated by one of the deceased victims
interacting and speaking with the wife of one of
the  co-accused,  against  whom  there  is  no
allegation  of  participation  in  the  physical
altercation. The specific allegation against the
petitioner is of shooting and killing one of the
abovementioned victims.
4. It is noted that the other co-accused who
were alleged to have participated in the fight
along with the petitioner, including one against
whom there are specific allegations of shooting
and killing the other two victims, have been
granted bail by the High Court. We are informed by
the Government Advocate that eight out of the ten
witnesses are examined.
5. Since the co-accused who are also alleged
with overt acts have been granted bail, and the
crucial prosecution witnesses have already been
examined,  we  are  of  the  opinion  that  the
petitioner too can be released on bail.
SLP (Crl.) No.14592/2026 3

## Page 561

6. On  a  prima  facie  consideration  of  the
material on record, we are of the opinion that the
petitioner can be released on bail, subject to
such terms and conditions that the District &
Additional  Sessions  Judge-I,  Seraikela  (the
jurisdictional court) may deem fit to impose. The
Petitioner shall cooperate with the trial.
7. With the above directions, the Special Leave
Petition is disposed of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also
stand disposed of.

        UPON hearing the counsel the Court made 
the following
                      O R D E R
1. The petitioner has been denied anticipatory
bail by the High Court in connection with FIR
No.18/2026 registered at PS WEA, District West
Tripura for the offence punishable under Sections
69, 89, 351, 49, and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 (for short “the BNS”).
2. The prosecutrix alleges several instances of
rape by the petitioner on multiple dates in 2024
and  2025,  after  entering  into  a  romantic
relationship  with  each  other.  It  is  further
alleged that on 29.03.2026, the petitioner and the
prosecutrix performed marriage rituals, but he
later backed out from it. It is also alleged that
he threatened to circulate intimate pictures of
the prosecutrix, and had also forced her to abort
her pregnancy. The petitioner’s parents have been
SLP (Crl.) No.14758/2026 2

## Page 564

made co-accused, alleging that they were privy to
his alleged misdeeds.
3. It is stated that the petitioner absconded
after he along with his parents were summoned to
the police station, and the accused persons sought
a few days’ time to take a decision.
4. The order impugned herein was challenged by
the learned Counsel for the petitioner on various
grounds,  including  that  this  is  a  consensual
romantic relationship gone awry, and that the
allegations in the FIR were absurd and improbable.
5. On  a  prima  facie  consideration  of  the
material on record, we are of the opinion that the
petitioner can be released on anticipatory bail.
We order that in the event of arrest of the
petitioner  in  connection  with  the  offence
enumerated above, he shall be released on bail,
subject to such terms and conditions that the
Investigating Officer (for short “I.O.”) may deem
fit to impose, on condition also of continued
cooperation in the investigation.

jurisdictional court and furnish bail bonds and
ensure due appearance in the trial.
7. With  the  aforesaid,  the  petition  stands
disposed of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, also stand

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. In pursuance of our last order dated 18.08.2026, the
parties are personally present in the Court today.
2. We heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties.
3. According  to  the  petitioner-husband,  he  has  paid
approximately an amount of Rs.41,00,000/- (Rupees Forty One
Lakh only) for the maintenance of his wife and his son over
a period of 14 years.
4. The learned counsel appearing for the respondent-wife
would submit that when the Court fixed an amount of
Rs.40,000/- (Rupees Forty thousand only) to be paid to
Tejas, i.e., the minor son, Court declined to pass any
order of maintenance so far as the wife is concerned.
However, in the D.V. proceedings, the Court awarded an
amount of Rs.50,000/- (Rupees Fifty thousand only) towards
maintenance of the wife and the son.
5. We  do  not  want  to  get  into  any  debate  whether
maintenance can be claimed from two different Courts under
two different legislations.
2

## Page 576

 Diary No. 22266/2025
6. Today, the proposal put forward by the wife is that she
is ready and willing to settle the entire dispute, if the
husband pays a lump-sump amount of Rs.30,00,000/- (Rupees
Thirty lakh only).  Her earnest appeal before the Court is,
that  the  marriage  be  dissolved  in  exercise  of  our
jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution.
7. We  have  made  ourselves  very  clear  before  the
petitioner-husband  that  the  amount  of  Rs.30,00,000/-
(Rupees Thirty lakh only) is reasonable.  He should accept
this proposal and put an end to the entire dispute.  We are
also ready and willing to dissolve the marriage.
8. Post this matter on 16.9.2026 at 10.30 A.M.
9. Parties are directed to personally remain present once
again on the next date of hearing, i.e., 16.9.2026.

2
No.385/2025 registered with Didauli Police Station,
District  Amroha,  Uttar  Pradesh,  for  the  offences
punishable under Section s 85, 103 & 115(2)  of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
2. Heard Mr. Mohd. Irshad Hanif, learned counsel for
the petitioner and Mr. Abhishek Saket, learned counsel
for the State.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the
petitioner has already undergone about 10 months in
custody.
4. We have been taken to the dying declaration and the
role attributed to the petitioner.
5. Learned counsel for the State Vehemently opposes the
bail prayer/application of the petitioner.
6. Considering the overall facts and circumstances of
the  case;  the  period  already  undergone  by  the
petitioner; the likelihood of the time taken by the
Trial Court to conclude the trial and also the fact
that petitioner is a woman, we extend the benefit of
bail to the petitioner, pending trial.
7. Accordingly, we direct that, pending trial,  the
petitioner shall be enlarged on bail subject to the
satisfaction of the concerned Trial Court in connection
with  the aforesaid FIR/Crime and for the offences
mentioned hereinabove.
8. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the
above terms.

2. The  present  Special  Leave  Petition  calls  in

passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur in
Misc.Criminal Case No.1655 of 2026. By the said order,
the High Court has denied the benefit of regular bail to
the petitioner in connection with FIR/Crime No.97 of 2025
dated 24 th December, 2025 registered at Police Station
Singhoda, District Mahasamund, Chhattisgarh for offence
punishable under Sections 20(B) and 29(1) of the Narcotic
Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985.
3. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner
submits that the petitioner has been implicated on the
statement of the co-accused.  Nothing has been recovered
from the conscious possession of the petitioner. The
petitioner has already undergone 7 months in custody,
since he was arrested on 20th January, 2026.  
4. Learned counsel for the respondent-State vehemently
opposes the contention of the petitioner for grant of
bail.
5. Considering the overall facts and circumstances,
the period of incarceration already undergone and the
fact that the fact that the trial is likely to take some
time to conclude and  keeping in mind the principles
enshrined in Article 21 of the Constitution of India as

Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 ,  we  direct
that pending trial, the petitioner shall be enlarged on

above terms.

disposed of.

CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE DIPANKAR DATTA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SHEEL NAGU
For Petitioner(s) : Ms. Prerna Singh, Adv.
                    Mr. Guntur Pramod Kumar, AOR
                    Mr. Arijeet Shukla, Adv.
                    Ms. Vanshika Singh, Adv.                   
                   
For Respondent(s) : Mr. V. Chitambaresh, Sr. Adv.
                    Ms. C. K. Sucharita, AOR
                    Mr. Vinod Kumar Gupta, Adv.
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The special leave petitions were presented before this Court 241 days
beyond the prescribed period of limitation. 
2. By an order dated 27 th February, 2026, a co-ordinate Bench of this Court
condoned the delay in presentation of the special leave petitions upon hearing
three of the several respondents who were appearing on caveat. Obviously, the
remaining respondents not having lodged any caveat, they were not heard.
1

## Page 593

3. In view of the provisions contained in Order XXI Rule 9(1) of the Supreme
Court Rules, 2013, delay in presentation of a belated special leave petition
cannot be condoned by a Bench without putting the respondents on notice. 
4. Insofar as the respondents who were not present before the Court are
concerned, Mr. V. Chitambaresh, learned senior counsel appearing on their
behalf is justified in urging that having regard to the false explanation proffered
in the application for condonation of delay, such order should be recalled and
the special leave petitions dismissed as time-barred. 
5. We have perused the application for condonation of delay and notice a
serious suppression on the part of the petitioners there.
6. Consequent upon disposal of the writ appeals 1 vide order dated 11 th
March, 2025 passed by the Division Bench of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh
at Amaravati2, a contempt petition3 was instituted by the respondents before a
Single Judge of the High Court. After a couple of adjournments were obtained,
the petitioners (being the contemnors before the Single Judge seized of the
contempt petition) sought for one final opportunity to comply with the order on
02nd January, 2026. It was accepting such request that the Single Judge
adjourned hearing till 06th February, 2026. It is, therefore, clear that the delayed
approach to this Court was not account of the cause shown in the application for
condonation of delay (the usual explanation of delay in obtaining approvals at
various levels) but delay was, in fact, caused by the petitioners themselves in
seeking adjournments in the proceedings for contempt and, in the process,
avoiding compliance with the impugned order. 
7. Ms. Prerna Singh, learned counsel appearing for the petitioners, submits
1 Writ Appeal Nos.890 of 2024 and 955 of 2024
2 High Court
3 CC No.3584 of 2024
2

## Page 594

that the order condoning delay has attained finality insofar as the caveators are
concerned and hence should not be recalled. 
8. Indeed, it is so; however, having regard to the nature of explanation
proffered in the application for condonation of delay which is completely far
from the truth, we invoke our inherent power and recall the order condoning
delay. 
9. We  are not  satisfied  that sufficient  cause has  been  shown.  The
interlocutory application4 seeking condonation of delay in presenting the special
leave petitions stands rejected; accordingly, the special leave petitions are
dismissed as time-barred. 
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
      (MANIK KUMAR)                         (SUDHIR KUMAR SHARMA)
SENIOR PERSONAL ASSISTANT                     COURT MASTER (NSH)
4 I. A. No.53369/2026

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. ______ OF 2026
[SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) Nos. 29138-29141 OF 2026]
RAM JIYAWAN MAURYA                           Appellant (s)
                                VERSUS
VIMAL YADAV & ORS.                           Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. These appeals are filed by the District Basic
Education Officer, Deoria, Uttar Pradesh against the
interim  order(s)  dated  16.07.2026  and  30.07.2026
passed  in  a  contempt  proceeding,  by  which  the
application  filed  by  the  respondents  seeking
correction of the order dated 29.05.2026, was allowed.
3. The facts giving rise to filing of these appeals
in a nutshell are that the respondents initiated a
proceeding of contempt for alleged non-compliance of
the order dated 04.12.2025, by which the High Court
had quashed the order of termination and had observed
that ‘the consequences to follow’. Liberty was granted
to the authorities to pass appropriate orders against
the respondent no.1 in accordance with law.
4. The High Court, in the said contempt proceeding,
passed an interim order dated 29.05.2026 directing
personal appearance of the appellant, if the order
directing  payment  of  salary  for  the  period  from

## Page 620

2
19.01.2026  to  14.05.2026,  is  not  complied  with.
Thereafter, by the impugned order dated 16.07.2026,
the said order was modified and the respondent no.1
was held entitled to the salary for the period from
which her appointment was cancelled.
5. Having heard learned counsel for the parties, in
our considered opinion, the High Court seems to have
travelled  beyond  the  limited  scope  of  contempt
jurisdiction by enlarging the scope of the substantive
order dated 04.12.2025 against which an action of
contempt  for  alleged  non-compliance  was  sought.
Therefore, the interim orders dated 16.07.2026 and
30.07.2026 are quashed and set aside. The direction
with regard to personal appearance of the appellant is
also set aside.
6. The High Court will now proceed with the contempt
petition on its own merits. We make it clear that we
have not expressed any opinion on the merits of the
case.
7. With these observations, the appeals are disposed
of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
Learned counsel appearing for the respondent has referred to
the order dated 13.10.2025 passed by the Court, whereby notice was
issued in the matter only for the limited purpose of exploring the
possibility of arriving at a settlement between the parties.
Learned counsel further submits that the Secretary/Commissioner,
Jaipur Development Authority, was asked to call for a meeting of
1

## Page 644

SLP(C) Nos. 30619-30620/2025
the parties and explore the possibilities of settlement and submit
a  report  thereupon.   However,  the  report  submitted  by  the
Secretary/Commissioner  states  that  no  agreement  or  settlement
reached between the parties.
At this, the learned counsel has also referred to the order
dated 24.02.2026 passed by Registrar’s Court, whereby taking the
submission of the learned counsel for the petitioner that a report
had been filed by the Secretary/Commissioner, Registry was directed
to process the matter for listing before the Court as per rules.
We find that the aforestated report is on record by way of
Affidavit of Compliance dated 20.02.2026.
In view of the above, learned counsel appearing for the
respondents urged that the matter be placed before the Court for
passing appropriate orders in the matter.
Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner submits that he
will cure the defects pointed out by the Registry, insofar as
application to bring on record legal heirs of deceased respondent
No. 4 in SLP(C) No. 30619/2025 and Affidavit of Compliance dated
20.02.2026 in SLP(C) No. 30620/2025 are concerned.
Needful in that regard shall be done within ten days from
today.
Having considered the submissions canvassed by the learned
counsel for the parties and perusing the earlier orders passed in
the matter, I am of the view that once notice was issued for the
limited purpose of exploring the possibility of settlement and when
such efforts have failed, the matter is required to be listed
2

## Page 645

SLP(C) Nos. 30619-30620/2025
before the Court for passing appropriate orders.
Registry shall, accordingly, process the matter for listing
before the Court on 09.09.2026.
