                             O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties. 
2. After  some  arguments,  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioners submits that in view of the order impugned
indicating that the permission to withdraw the Suit and
the revision petition, with liberty to file a fresh suit
before the appropriate forum, it is being construed as
meaning that the delay in filing the said Suit would
stand condoned. It was submitted that this ambiguity has
arisen because of the High Court observing such liberty
to file fresh suit before appropriate forum as mentioned
in the application itself, where one of the prayers asked
was also for condonation of limitation.
3. Thus, it was prayed by learned counsel for the
petitioners that he may be permitted to withdraw the
present petition with liberty to seek clarification/
modification/review of the order impugned. Further, it
was submitted that, if required, the petitioner may be
given further liberty to move this Court thereafter, in
case such need arises.
4. Having regard to the aforesaid, the petition stands
disposed of as withdrawn with liberty aforesaid.
5. However, we clarify that we have not expressed any
2

SLP (C)  NO.24417/2025
opinion with regard to the merits of the matter, which
shall be independently considered by the Court concerned.

weeks from today, the interim protection given to the
petitioners  by  this  Court  under  the  order  dated
22.08.2025  and  as  extended  from  time  to  time  shall
continue till the disposal of the review petition.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

been appointed only in the year 2020 and having completed
only three years of service as on the date the Writ
Petition(s) was decided by learned Single Judge, there is no
question of regularization within three years of service.
Even otherwise, the Writ Petitioners were Zila Parishad
employees and not the Government employees.
7. Having  heard  learned  counsel  for  the  parties,  we
dispose  of  these  petitions  observing  that  the  issue
regarding regularization was neither prayed nor considered
properly by the Writ Court and therefore, there was no need
for any observations concerning regularization of the Writ
Petitioners. If the Writ Petitioners are covered under any
scheme of regularization floated by the State Government,
they would be at liberty to agitate the issue afresh in
separate proceedings.
8. With the aforesaid observations, the Special Leave
Petitions are disposed of.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of. 
  (VISHAL ANAND)                              (AKSHAY KUMAR BHORIA)

## Page 761

were stayed by the learned Single Judge on 24.04.2026. The
Union of India thereafter, has filed LPA No. 336/2026 in
the matter and the same was decided on 26.05.2026, vacating
the interim order granting by the learned Single Judge. 
2. In the meanwhile, the Estate Officer has passed
eviction order on 11.08.2026 and thereafter, an appeal has
been  preferred  in  the  matter  before  the  District
Judge/appellate authority and at the same time, the present
Special Leave Petition has also been filed on 13.08.2026.
3. The facts remain that appeal is pending before the
District Judge/appellate authority. Learned Senior counsel
appearing for the petitioner has informed this Court that
because of the pendency of the present appeal, the learned
District Judge/appellate authority has not decided the
application for grant of stay and from tomorrow onwards,
the courts are closed for three days. 
4. In the considered opinion of this Court, as an
appeal has been preferred in the matter, we do not find any
reason to interfere in the present Special Leave Petition.
However,  the  appellate  authority  shall  decide  the
application without being influenced by the order passed by
the learned Single Judge as well as by the Division Bench,
in accordance with law. 
5. So far as the application for grant of interim
relief  is  concerned,  the  same  is  pending  before  the
District Judge/appellate authority, and the parties are

authority today itself for preponement of hearing and the

Leave Petition stands dismissed. 
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

Learned counsel for the respondent/State submitted 
that the investigation is still on and if some time is 
granted, the Investigating Officer (I.O.) shall conclude 
the investigation in the matter.  Further, the petitioner
is also cooperating in the investigation.  
In the circumstances, we adjourn this matter to  
28.09.2026.
Interim order to  continue till the next date of 
hearing.
We also clarify that the interim order granted by us 
would not come in the way of the I.O. continuing with the
investigation and taking steps in accordance with the 
evidence collected during the course of investigation.  
However, the interim order would imply that no arrest of 
the petitioner would be made. Hence, we have used the 
expression “no coercive steps shall be taken as against 
the petitioner herein provided he cooperates with the 
investigation” 
We also say that any interim protection granted by 
this Court in the matter of anticipatory bail does not 
2

## Page 765

imply that on conclusion of the investigation if the  
necessity arises for filing of a charge sheet, the same 
is also barred. In other words, once the investigation is
concluded and charge sheet has to be filed, the I.O. is 
always at liberty to do so in accordance with law and any
interim order granted by any Court  during the course of 
consideration of a case for anticipatory bail would only 
imply that the liberty  of  the  person  seeking  
anticipatory bail is protected.

opinion that the petitioner should have the benefit of  pre-
arrest bail.

petitioner shall be released on anticipatory bail subject to
the satisfaction of the concerned Investigating Officer in

Nadu,  for  the  offences  punishable  under  Sections  296(B),

under Sections 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 and under
Section 4 of Tamil Nadu Prohibition of Harassment of Woman Act,
1998.

terms.

are now concerned with the present litigation.

returnable on 22.09.2026.

## Page 1065

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
The petitioner is an accused in Complaint Case Nos.419392/2025,
328686/2025 and NACT/6481/2025. He is facing charges under Section 223 of
the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and Section 138 read with Section
142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 in the complaint filed by the
respondent – Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd.
2. Ms. Kamlesh, learned counsel appearing for the petitioner refers to
Jurisdiction Clause vide Clause No.12.10 of the agreement which provides that
“the Courts in the State where the Agreement is executed shall have exclusive
jurisdiction in relation to this Agreement, the arbitration in all matters
connected herewith and therewith…”.
3. Ms. Kamlesh, learned counsel for the petitioner further refers to the
agreement signed between the parties and submits that initiation of criminal
proceedings at various places across the country is an abuse of the process of
the Court.
4. The Jurisdiction Clause vide Clause No.12.10 can be a ground for
challenging the civil proceedings instituted at a place which is not the place
where the agreement was executed or the arbitration or any other matter
connected therewith had commenced. By virtue of Clause No.12.10, the
jurisdiction of a criminal court is not excluded.
5. Transfer Petitions are, accordingly, dismissed.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner is aggrieved by an amendment in the Mizo
Marriage, Divorce and Inheritance of Property Act, 2014, which has
been carried out by the Mizoram Legislative Assembly. 
2. In our considered opinion, there is no necessity for the
petitioner to approach this Court directly, as the grievance can be
effectively redressed by the jurisdictional High Court.
3. The petitioner's apprehension that the matter may not be heard
1

## Page 1135

at Aizawl Bench, owing to the charged atmosphere, can also be
effectively addressed by requesting the Hon'ble Chief Justice of
the Gauhati High Court to list the matter before the Principal
Bench at Gauhati.
4. Further, the issue raised on behalf of the petitioner prima
facie  requires preferential attention. However, we do not express
any opinion on merits of the case at this stage. 
5. The instant petition is, thus, disposed of with liberty to the
petitioner to approach the Principal Bench of the Gauhati High
Court, where her writ petition may be entertained in light of the
observations made hereinabove.
6. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

1. Delay condoned.

the development of a dedicated South Container Berth at Paradip
Port on a Build-Operate-Transfer basis through a Public-Private
Partnership. Respondent nos.1 and 2 also participated in the

## Page 1143

bidding  process.  However,  vide  disqualification  notice  dated
22.09.2025, their application was rejected and categorized as “non-
qualified”.
3. Aggrieved by the aforesaid decision, the private respondents
approached the High Court of Orissa by way of Writ Petition No.
26886/2025, wherein the High Court passed a self-speaking interim
order dated 25.09.2025, restraining the petitioners authorities
from proceeding further pursuant to the tender process.
4. That order is now being challenged before us.
5. It is not in dispute that the matter is pending before the
High Court.
6. We are informed that the matter was last taken up in May 2026.
7. Since finalization of tender has been stalled, we request the
High Court to take up Writ Petition(C) No. 26886/2025 and decide
the  same  at  the  earliest,  as  the  controversy  pertains  to
development of an infrastructural project.
8. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly, disposed of.
9. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This writ petition was filed in the year 2020 seeking a
direction for premature release of the petitioner in accordance
with law. Admittedly, the instant petitioner is a life convict,
having been convicted on 12.12.1994 in a case under Section 302 of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860. 
2. The petitioner was 99 years old when the petition was filed in
the year 2020, and is now reported to be 105 years of age. On
29.11.2024, the petitioner was directed to be released on interim
bail/parole during pendency of these proceedings.
3. Having regard to the petitioner’s age, we see no justification
1

## Page 1277

for not releasing the petitioner prematurely, even if he has not
completed the entire period of sentence.
4. Consequently, the writ petition is disposed of. The interim
order dated 29.11.2024 is made absolute, and it is directed that
the petitioner shall be treated as having been prematurely released
for all intents and purposes.
5. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The instant writ petition has been filed primarily seeking two
reliefs: first, permission for medical termination of the pregnancy
of the minor rape victim; and second, a direction to the Union of
India to frame guidelines constituting qualified Medical Boards in
all the States and Union of Territories to decide cases of medical
termination of pregnancy beyond 20 weeks, particularly in cases of
1

## Page 1299

rape  by  blood  relatives  where  there  is  a  risk  of  foetal
abnormality. 
2. Learned Additional Solicitor General of India informs us that
after receipt of notice in this petition, the Medial Termination of
Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 and the Medical Termination of
Pregnancy Rules, 2003 have been suitably amended on 24.09.2021 and
10.06.2024 respectively.  
3. In light of these subsequent events, we are hopeful that the
prayer (ii) has been effectively addressed. However, whether these
Amendments have proved to be effective or the victims are still
facing hardship due to time-limit prescriptions, is an issue to be
examined on a case to case basis.
4. Liberty is granted to learned counsel for the petitioner to
file an appropriate petition for the desired relief, wherever such
an instance has come to their notice.
5. With liberty aforementioned, the Writ Petition is disposed of.
6. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
(ARJUN BISHT)                              (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

case, we grant further time of 30 days to the petitioner from today
to deposit the amount of 10,00,000/- (Rupees Ten Lakhs Only)₹
before the Trial Magistrate as directed by the High Court.

The suit was dismissed by the Trial Court by Judgment and decree
dated 20-12-2023, against which some of the parties preferred
Regular First Appeal No.79 of 2024. However, during the pendency of
the same, Indramma, who was already arrayed as one of the legal
heirs of deceased Doddamunyappa, preferred WP No.16046 of 2024
under Article 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India which
appears to have been treated by the High Court as a petition under
Article 227 only and in the said petition, the present impugned
order  has  been  passed  reserving  liberty  in  favour  of  the
Respondents to prefer an application under Order 23 Rule 3A of the
Civil Procedure Code before the same Court which recorded the
compromise.
5. It  is  next  submitted  that  some  other  legal  heirs  of
Doddamunyappa preferred RFA No.79 of 2024, which has been dismissed
by the High Court. Therefore, the compromise decree having been
upheld in the subsequent suit, the liberty granted by the High
Court in the present impugned Order is of no avail as the Trial
Court would be bound by the Order passed in RFA No.79/2024.
6. Issue notice to the Respondents, returnable in eight weeks.
7. In the meanwhile, the effect and operation of the impugned
Orders passed by the High Court is stayed.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. The petitioner who had been denied bail by the High Court, has
been in judicial custody since 19.09.2025, which is a period of
more than 11 months, in connection with FIR No. 10/2025 dated
25.04.2025 registered at PS Cyber Crime, District Howrah Rural,
West Bengal for the offence punishable under Sections 318(2),
318(4), 319(2), 336(3), 61(2), 316(2), 317(4), 338, 340(2), 351(2),
and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (for short “the BNS”) and
Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (for
short “the IT Act”).

## Page 1567

2
3. The allegations arise from the complainant being subject to a
digital arrest scam, in which the complainant is said to have sent
a total of Rs. 41,44,357/- (Rupees Forty-One Lakhs Forty-Four
Thousand Three Hundred and Fifty-Seven Only) online. The specific
allegation against the petitioner is from the money trail; an
account operated in the name of a company owned by the petitioner
is said to have received an amount of Rs. 17,60,000/- (Rupees
Seventeen Lakhs Sixty Thousand Only), which is said to have been
further transferred to multiple beneficiary accounts on the very
same day. 
4. Supplementary Chargesheet was filed on 04.12.2025, in which
the petitioner’s name was mentioned. 
5. The petitioner has been in custody for about an year. Hence,
there  is  no  requirement  for  further  custodial  interrogation,
especially since the chargesheet has been filed.
6.On a prima facie consideration of the material on record, we are
of the opinion that the petitioner can be released on bail, subject
to such terms and conditions that the Chief Judicial Magistrate,
Chandannagar (the jurisdictional court) may deem fit to impose. The
petitioner shall cooperate with the trial. 
7. With the above directions, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of. 
8.  Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The issue with respect to implementation of Mahatma Gandhi
National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 (MGNREGA) has been
effectively answered by this Court in Swaraj  Abhiyan  v. Union  of
India & Ors., (2016) 7 SCC 498.
1

## Page 1617

2. We may also hasten to add that MGNREGA has now been replaced
by a new legislation, i.e. Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and
Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (“VB–G RAM G”).
3. We, therefore, dispose of this petition in light of the
decision in Swaraj Abhiyan ( supra) with liberty to the petitioners
to file an appropriate petition with respect to the statutory
scheme as contained in the VB-G RAM G, including on the issue of
grant of minimum wages.  
4. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand closed.

2. According  to  prosecution’s  case,  petitioner  was
carrying a lathi, whereas, the postmortem report records
cause of death was shock and hemorrhage due to fire-arm
injuries.

case including the nature and quality of evidence against
the petitioner, we are inclined to suspend the sentence and
release the petitioner on bail, in connection with FIR
No.320 of 1982 registered at Police Station – Konch,
District – Jalaun for offences punishable under  Sections
147, 149, 302 and 307 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 o n
such terms and conditions as may be imposed by the Trial
Court, subject to the condition that the petitioner shall
co-operate with the trial.
4. Accordingly, the Special Leave Petition is disposed
of.

disposed of.

 On interaction with the learned counsel for the parties, it
appears that the matter can be amicably settled between the
parties.
In such circumstances, the parties are directed to appear
before  the  Coordinator,  Supreme  Court  Mediation  Centre  on
11.09.2026 at 11.00 a.m. The Coordinator is requested to appoint a
Senior Mediator to enable the parties to make an effort to settle
the matter amicably.
Initially, the parties are permitted to appear virtually and
thereafter, the parties shall appear as per the directions of the
Mediator.
